1978-06-zigzag-doll-by-doll-acne-club-ay.titel: [Short review of Doll by Doll, Acne Club, Aylesbury] ("URGENT!! The proverbial hold-the-presses review!")
1978-06-zigzag-doll-by-doll-acne-club-ay.kurz: Kris Needs' first encounter with Doll by Doll, hurriedly slotted into the issue: while Steve Hillage plays the Friars Club, he sees the band in front of 40 to 50 people in the back room of a pub in Aylesbury that presents up-and-coming bands on Wednesdays as the “Acne Club”.
inhalt: Kris Needs' first encounter with Doll by Doll, hurriedly slotted into the issue: while Steve Hillage plays the Friars Club, he sees the band in front of 40 to 50 people in the back room of a pub in Aylesbury that presents up-and-coming bands on Wednesdays as the “Acne Club”. After the set Leven apologises to the audience for what he says was a bad night; Needs is overwhelmed, makes cautious comparisons with the Stranglers, Television and West Coast rock, and stresses the band's originality. He mentions the titles “Guts” and “Butcher Boy”, that the band live in a London squat, donate their fees to an American charity and have turned down record companies, and announces a major profile for the next issue (the later piece in ZigZag No. 92). Tone: hymnic.

1978-10-21-music-week-automatic-signs-do.titel: [News items: first signing for Nick Mobbs' Automatic Record Company / “Automatic signings”]

1978-11-18-record-mirror-chris-westwood-.titel: [Band profile with interview: “Chris Westwood dresses Doll By Doll up”]
1978-11-18-record-mirror-chris-westwood-.kurz: One-page Record Mirror profile in which Chris Westwood – later the band's most important champion at Record Mirror – introduces Doll by Doll ahead of the release of their debut.
inhalt: One-page Record Mirror profile in which Chris Westwood – later the band's most important champion at Record Mirror – introduces Doll by Doll ahead of the release of their debut. He begins with the lower-case spelling after E. E. Cummings that Leven adopted, and places the band on an axis running from Cochran and Holly through the Velvet Underground into something of the future. Automatic Records, Nick Mobbs' new project, signed Doll by Doll as its first band; as the piece is written, Leven (guitar, vocals), David McIntosh (drums), Robin Spreafico (bass) and Jo Shaw (guitar) are working on the album. The interview took place in the band's squat in Maida Vale near Warwick Avenue tube station, though only with Shaw and McIntosh. Shaw explains the connection with the Philadelphia Association (shared houses for people in psychological crisis, inspired by R. D. Laing's ideas): the band played benefit concerts and donated part of the Automatic advance, but the connection has been exaggerated in other articles – as has the influence of Artaud, who mainly inspired Leven. McIntosh says that about two and a half years earlier he played with Leven in Dorset in another band that never performed; after it ended he went abroad, and then Shaw, Leven, Spreafico and he found each other – about a year ago. Since then almost a hundred concerts, support slots for John Otway and Ultravox, and next the Devo tour with two nights at the Hammersmith Odeon. Both talk about the risk on stage (“like a tightrope”). Leven's earlier album, available only in Spain, is also mentioned. Tone: enthusiastic, presenting the band as a genuine, uncompromising alternative to commercialised punk.

1979-03-zigzag-night-of-the-psychotic-wo.kurz: Major Doll by Doll piece by Kris Needs shortly before the release of the debut album *Remember* (23 March 1979), nine months after the first interview in ZigZag No. 85. Needs raves about the album, which was recorded live, apart from a few overdubs, at Wessex Studios with Bill Price, describes “Sleeping Par…
inhalt: Major Doll by Doll piece by Kris Needs shortly before the release of the debut album *Remember* (23 March 1979), nine months after the first interview in ZigZag No. 85. Needs raves about the album, which was recorded live, apart from a few overdubs, at Wessex Studios with Bill Price, describes “Sleeping Partner”, “Chances”, “Janice”, “More Than Human” and “Palace of Love” (as a shortened single, because “Teenage Lightning” could no longer be pulled off after three attempts). He recounts the path since summer 1978: ZigZag as a port of call for record companies, the contract with Nick Mobbs' Automatic (WEA distribution), being thrown off the Devo tour after two concerts (“not Devo enough”), the band still living in a squatted house in Maida Vale (“Hard Ventures HQ”). Leven is annoyed about an advance review in *Sounds*. In conversation, over whisky, Leven (and Jo Shaw) explain that the band are “amateur”, its members “all fucked up”, standing outside political camps and rock clichés. Then the interview turns dark: Leven speaks of a “death trip” of the band, predicts his own end “within the next three LPs”, compares himself to Sid Vicious (whom he knew from Maida Vale) and tells of a suicide attempt before Christmas 1978. The next day in the pub he is relaxed again; at night Needs listens to Leven's “Spanish only” solo album (*Control*). Outlook: tours, a second album in the autumn, new songs such as “Hell Game” and “An Honest Woman”. Tone: fanlike, moved.
zitate_kontext: Leven on the band on stage.

1979-05-05-record-mirror-chris-westwood-.titel: [Tour report with interview: “communication that only some have heard”]
1979-05-05-record-mirror-chris-westwood-.kurz: Chris Westwood's second major Record Mirror story, written on the spring 1979 tour after the release of “Remember”.
inhalt: Chris Westwood's second major Record Mirror story, written on the spring 1979 tour after the release of “Remember”. The starting point is the recent pannings in the rock press, to which the band, by their own account, reacted almost with relief: Dave McIntosh says they had expected a kicking sooner or later, and that the criticism had welded the band back together. Westwood attacks a critic who, after earlier praise, has now torn into Leven's songs, singing and guitar playing – two of the passages praised as Jo Shaw solos were in fact played by Leven; Leven mockingly calls the journalist “a human with a pencil”. There follow ironic mini-biographies of the members (Spreafico as a “Dutch peasant” who keeps silent about the past; Leven with “three divorces, five months in jail”; Shaw with a boarding-school past in Fort Augustus), a concert scene at the York Pop Club, where the punk audience reacts with unease to the open emotionality, and long Leven passages: on the “death trip” from the ZigZag interview, the lack of understanding of death in the modern world, the “war” over whether people will ever feel one another, and the announcement that the band will change radically – the new songs “Forbidden Lands” and “The Hell Games” already lead away. Westwood confesses that the band have fundamentally changed his attitude to rock. Tone: avowedly partisan.
zitate_kontext: Leven against the charge of morbidity.

1979-07-zigzag-zigzag-10th-birthday-part.titel: [Report from the ZigZag birthday party at the Venue, London – excerpts on Doll by Doll]
1979-07-zigzag-zigzag-10th-birthday-part.kurz: Excerpts from Kris Needs' report on the party for ZigZag's tenth anniversary at the Venue in London (June 1979).
inhalt: Excerpts from Kris Needs' report on the party for ZigZag's tenth anniversary at the Venue in London (June 1979). Doll by Doll play a specially put-together set of old pub numbers (“Stripshow”, “Honest Woman”, “Palace of Love”), are annoyed by the drinking, chattering audience and work themselves up to extreme volume; at the end Jo Shaw smashes a valuable guitar. The thank-you list stresses that the Doll by Doll crew (road manager Colin from the “Dolls House”) helped organise the party for weeks. Tone: enthusiastic and partisan.

1979-09-01-record-mirror-reading-festiva.kurz: Westwood's report on the Friday of the 1979 Reading Festival (24.08.1979, headliners The Police).
inhalt: Westwood's report on the Friday of the 1979 Reading Festival (24.08.1979, headliners The Police). Doll by Doll were the whipping boys, hated by almost everyone so much that the crowd was able to let off steam early; Leven later said that every band serves a function in this absurd spectacle. Westwood regrets that the band were put into this entirely unsuitable setting and came out again without any sympathy; The Cure were the most impressive band. Tone: critical of the festival, in solidarity with Doll by Doll.

1979-11-17-record-mirror-doll-by-doll-mu.kurz: Live review of a concert at the Music Machine in London (autumn 1979). Westwood distinguishes Doll by Doll from other “expressionists”: the band do what they must, not what they want; their music of fear, violence and romance (“Butcher Boy”, “The Human Face”, “Palace of Love”) is communication rather than pose.
inhalt: Live review of a concert at the Music Machine in London (autumn 1979). Westwood distinguishes Doll by Doll from other “expressionists”: the band do what they must, not what they want; their music of fear, violence and romance (“Butcher Boy”, “The Human Face”, “Palace of Love”) is communication rather than pose. The performance was unusually relaxed and free of shock moments; the band are “the realest” he has ever seen, but need time, which the rock business gives no one. Tone: hymnic.

1979-11-17-record-mirror-gypsy-blood-gyp.kurz: Contemporary review of the second album by Chris Westwood, which at the same time defends the debut: “Remember” was slated by form-obsessed critics although it was a very powerful record of disturbing honesty.
inhalt: Contemporary review of the second album by Chris Westwood, which at the same time defends the debut: “Remember” was slated by form-obsessed critics although it was a very powerful record of disturbing honesty. “Gypsy Blood” seems almost relaxed on the surface but is subtle and deceptively accessible; Westwood singles out Jo Shaw's “Endgame”, which is about Shaw's experiences of the heroin scene. Rating: high (stars not legible in the scan), tone enthusiastic. In the same issue (p. 31) Westwood's live review from the Music Machine.

inhalt: The fan tape “PM209” in the Peel wiki lists for the broadcast of 22 November 1979 “Teenage Lightning” by Doll by Doll (opening track of “Gypsy Blood”) alongside a Comsat Angels session, Errol Dunkley and the Dickies. A further find: the fan tape “Karl's Tape September 1982” (peel.fandom.com/wiki/Karl%27s_Tape_September_1982) contains “Under My Thumb” (Magnet MAG 225), though it remains unclear whether from a Peel or a Kid Jensen show.

1979-12-29-record-mirror-doll-by-doll-u2.kurz: Contemporary review of the concert of 18.12.1979 at the Venue in London, at which U2, then barely known in England, played in support.
inhalt: Contemporary review of the concert of 18.12.1979 at the Venue in London, at which U2, then barely known in England, played in support. Westwood despises the club (table service, fruit machines, polite applause as in variety theatre). He describes U2 very positively: Bono as a uniquely expressive frontman, the witty line from the first “Cabaret” appearance, a band that has mastered dynamics. Doll by Doll are harder to explain; they played twelve songs, including “The Fountain Is Red”, “An Honest Woman”, “Hell Games” and “Palace of Love”, a restrained, good-humoured set that Westwood experiences as a quiet vindication. Tone: hymnic for both bands. Photo caption: Jackie Leven and Tony Waite.

1981-06-08-record-business-doll-by-doll-.titel: [Album review] Doll By Doll: Doll By Doll (Magnet MAGL5039)
1981-06-08-record-business-doll-by-doll-.kurz: Trade review of the third album (production Tom Newman/Jackie Leven): quite a U-turn for the band, who are now continuing their search for media acceptance at Magnet.
inhalt: Trade review of the third album (production Tom Newman/Jackie Leven): quite a U-turn for the band, who are now continuing their search for media acceptance at Magnet. They now sound fashionably psychedelic, with ethereal guitar harmonics and steady Teardrop Explodes-style drumming, but cannot hide the power in the voices of Leven and “Joe” Shaw, which make even melancholy material sound urgent. That Doll by Doll were among the first in this genre might help them this time. Tone: benevolent. In the airplay overview of the same issue, “Main Travelled Roads” appears in the playlists.

1981-06-13-music-week-doll-by-doll-album.titel: [Album and single review] Doll By Doll: Doll By Doll (Magnet MAGL 5039) / Main Travelled Roads (MAG 188)
1981-06-13-music-week-doll-by-doll-album.kurz: Two trade reviews in the same issue: the third album (producers: Tom Newman and Jackie Leven), the first on Magnet, offers rock with dreamy-romantic lyrics that provokes divided and at times heated reactions – you love it or hate it; some songs sound strangely old-fashioned at first, but grow on repeated listening; with tours and a single it could sell well. The single “Main Travelled Roads” (MAG 188): strong live band, dramatic ballad, pleasant effect, but without a hook that sticks. The gossip column mentions a party at the Venue for the band's Magnet signing.
inhalt: Two trade reviews in the same issue: the third album (producers: Tom Newman and Jackie Leven), the first on Magnet, offers rock with dreamy-romantic lyrics that provokes divided and at times heated reactions – you love it or hate it; some songs sound strangely old-fashioned at first, but grow on repeated listening; with tours and a single it could sell well. The single “Main Travelled Roads” (MAG 188): strong live band, dramatic ballad, pleasant effect, but without a hook that sticks. The gossip column mentions a party at the Venue for the band's Magnet signing.

1981-06-15-record-business-doll-by-doll-.kurz: Short live review of a Monday concert at the Venue in London in June 1981. Hayward wonders that the band, who held on to their own rock 'n' roll for so long, are now getting the “psychedelic” label.
inhalt: Short live review of a Monday concert at the Venue in London in June 1981. Hayward wonders that the band, who held on to their own rock 'n' roll for so long, are now getting the “psychedelic” label. New material from the Magnet album was presented, revolving around Leven's folk roots, with explosive feedback guitars from Jo Shaw. “Main Travelled Roads” was given a prominent place, but the full house responded more strongly to harder numbers such as “I Never Saw The Movie” and “The Street I Love”. Tone: benevolent; the strong following should finally be rewarded with album success.

1981-06-20-record-mirror-crystal-balls-u.kurz: Disappointed live review of the same Venue concert of June 1981 that Record Business (15.06.1981) reviewed benevolently.
inhalt: Disappointed live review of the same Venue concert of June 1981 that Record Business (15.06.1981) reviewed benevolently. Smith says that after so long underground he had expected an earthquake and got only a few tremors. Leven seemed irritable and played the shy, sensitive artist; the old manic style that pinned you to your seat had largely disappeared. Old pieces such as “Palace of Love” were missing, “Main Travelled Roads” was brutally cut short. Verdict: decent, but not inspired; 1981 and the new contract would decide the band's future. Tone: negative.

1982-12-02-34th-street-doll-by-doll-gran.titel: [Album review] Doll By Doll – Grand Passion (Magnet, UK)
1982-12-02-34th-street-doll-by-doll-gran.kurz: One of the few US reviews of Doll by Doll, preserved as a transcript on the author's site.
inhalt: One of the few US reviews of Doll by Doll, preserved as a transcript on the author's site. Silverman writes that the virtually unknown band have been releasing near-classic albums for four years for an indifferent public, and that this will not change without a big Magnet campaign. He praises Leven's melodies, which sound classic at once, and the voice to match, compares “Cool Skies” and “Lonely Kind of Show” with Steely Dan, Roxy Music and early Dylan/Beatles, singles out “Natural” and the war image “City of Light”, and finds the “Under My Thumb” cover credible. His only objection: Leven's humourless pursuit of the “grand passion” grows tiring and borders on melodrama. Tone: strongly positive; number 6 on his 1982 year-end list.

1983-01-17-record-business-doll-by-doll-.kurz: Report on Doll by Doll's last London concert on a Friday evening at the Marquee (January 1983), in front of many of the faithful from the “optimistic days of Automatic”.
inhalt: Report on Doll by Doll's last London concert on a Friday evening at the Marquee (January 1983), in front of many of the faithful from the “optimistic days of Automatic”. The emotionally charged Leven is said to be determined to close the Doll by Doll chapter of his life, and wants to retreat to the Outer Hebrides to write new songs and return with a new persona, probably at a new label – underlined by a rocking version of the “Skye Boat Song”. Instead of old favourites and the Magnet repertoire, the band played mainly new rock songs; “Cool Skies” and “Dancing Shoes” represented “Grand Passion”, with co-vocalist and keyboard player Helen Turner in good voice; Leven himself played lead guitar. It is regretted that the band, entirely their own, never found national recognition. Tone: wistful and appreciative.

1990-10-10-nursing-standard-core-trust-d.titel: [News item: CORE Trust Day Centre for drug addicts opens in London]

1990-12-the-company-the-core-trust-fish.kurz: The former Marillion singer Fish writes in the first person about his friendship with Leven and about the CORE Trust.
inhalt: The former Marillion singer Fish writes in the first person about his friendship with Leven and about the CORE Trust. He says he met Leven in the bar of the Marquee in Wardour Street, in the middle of his own “Incommunicado” phase; in the conversations of the following years the subject kept returning to Leven's idea of a clinic that would treat not only the body but the soul of those suffering from addiction. Fish contrasts this with the government's anti-heroin advertising campaign, which he criticises as superficial, and says he donated at Leven's request. Through Judy Totten, a CORE PR consultant, he met the New Zealand acupuncturist Murray Douglas in 1987; a large part of the text is a testimony to acupuncture, hypnotherapy, Bach flower remedies and medicinal herbs. On Leven: a Scot “through to the core”, formerly the frontman of an underrated band, who came to CORE after his own drug problems; he is no longer involved in the clinic, and the last Fish heard was that Leven was in Australia preparing a career as a poet and singer. CORE is now run by Carol Wolf, who founded the Trust with Leven; the centre in Lisson Cottages (Lisson Grove) has been renovated and was reopened by Princess Diana on 19 September, and the WHO is interested in the model. The text ends with an appeal for donations.

1991-08-31-nme-great-lost-albums-doll-by.kurz: Stuart Maconie presents the third, self-titled Doll by Doll album (Magnet 1981) as his personal “lost album”: uninfluential and barely heard, but loved by him.
inhalt: Stuart Maconie presents the third, self-titled Doll by Doll album (Magnet 1981) as his personal “lost album”: uninfluential and barely heard, but loved by him. He praises Leven's guitar playing and the versatile voice, singles out “Up”, “Bright Green Field”, “Main Travelled Roads” and “Caritas”, and asks at the end where the band have gone – readers with information or a good copy should get in touch. Tone: affectionate hymn; he calls the follow-up album weaker.

1994-08-10-arbeiderbladet-mektig-og-jord.kurz: Positive short review of the solo debut: Leven spent the last decade more with the withdrawal treatment of fellow musicians (CORE Trust) than with his career – credit to him for that, especially as the album is bigger than most of what is on the market.
inhalt: Positive short review of the solo debut: Leven spent the last decade more with the withdrawal treatment of fellow musicians (CORE Trust) than with his career – credit to him for that, especially as the album is bigger than most of what is on the market. Praise goes to the “cinemascopic” breadth of sound made of mandolins, violins, synthesizers and electric guitars and above all the voice, which is crooner, folk and soul singer in one. He sings “I Say a Little Prayer” with Scott Walker elegance, and the rest are slow, lyrical originals.

1995-01-04-nordlands-framtid-kraftig-og-.kurz: Belated review of the solo debut in the Bodø newspaper: in the early 80s Leven led Doll by Doll, a critically praised but commercially unsuccessful soul-rock band; Mike Scott as helper shows the direction.
inhalt: Belated review of the solo debut in the Bodø newspaper: in the early 80s Leven led Doll by Doll, a critically praised but commercially unsuccessful soul-rock band; Mike Scott as helper shows the direction. Expansive, powerful sound, thoughtful lyrics, pop, rock and folk combined, Leven's voice carrying the melodies – one of the records of ’94 that should not be overlooked.

1995-02-02-fremtiden-jackie-leven-er-til.kurz: By its own account the first and only Norwegian newspaper interview with Leven after his comeback (Fremtiden 03.05.1995).
inhalt: By its own account the first and only Norwegian newspaper interview with Leven after his comeback (Fremtiden 03.05.1995). Andreassen had put *The Mystery of Love* in third place on his 1994 year-end list. Leven tells the story of the attack like this: at two in the morning he left the studio and wanted to walk home, was attacked and almost strangled, for two or three years he could neither speak nor sing, and he endured a severe depression only with constant heroin; years of training in the “Alexander Technique” repaired his voice. He describes the centre he founded, The Core Trust, which treats all kinds of addiction with acupuncture, among other things.

On his helpers: Mike Scott later rescued the Core project with badly needed money, and a joint album is under discussion; Robert Bly he has admired since he was 16 and regards as the greatest performer of his time. Leven left Scotland as a teenager to escape gangs and fights; on his return he found a changed country with a better relationship between women and men, and Scottish men now had to free themselves from English dominance. He sees close ties between Norway and Scotland (Shetland, the north-east), hopes for a tour or an Oslo concert in early March with his keyboard friend “James Halliway”, and announces the next album, *The Year I Left My Heart*, for April – he has asked Van Morrison to take part.
zitate_kontext: Leven on the evening of the attack.

1995-03-10-the-big-untidy-jackie-leven-i.kurz: Long fanzine interview, conducted backstage at the Pfefferberg in Berlin on 10.03.1995, shortly before Leven introduced Andy White; on tour with keyboard player James Hallawell for the EP with “I Say A Little Prayer”.
inhalt: Long fanzine interview, conducted backstage at the Pfefferberg in Berlin on 10.03.1995, shortly before Leven introduced Andy White; on tour with keyboard player James Hallawell for the EP with “I Say A Little Prayer”. The introduction sums up Doll by Doll, the attack, heroin and the return to Oban and the west coast, praises *The Mystery Of Love…* and *Songs From The Argyll Cycle*, reports on the Cooking Vinyl package tour with Tom Robinson and Andy White at the Knaack in Berlin (October 1994) and mentions CORE (acronym spelt out), the men's movement around Robert Bly and the whisky “Leven's Lament”.

In conversation Leven says: Doll by Doll (founded ’76/’77) fell between two stools – too heavy for punk's opponents, not punk for punks; he regards punk as a middle-class phenomenon. The band broke up because nobody bought the records. He describes the attack here without embellishment: drunk, walking from the studio near the Caledonian Road to Maida Vale, “just got mugged”. Afterwards about two years without a voice, steroids (“electric fur”), isolation, heroin, which he describes as a journey of initiation. He developed the CORE Trust out of his own withdrawal programme, with his girlfriend Carol, who was in the last Doll by Doll line-up, on the advice of her homeopathic doctor. He came to Cooking Vinyl through his lawyer, who recommended Martin Goldschmidt. He says he was the first schoolboy in Scotland to be caught for drugs and discovered Bly in the school library; he explains the Dylan co-authorship of “As We Sailed Into Skibbereen” with a shared train journey from Berlin to St Petersburg. Finally, explanations of “Call Mother A Lonely Field” (ploughed winter fields) and “The Garden” (Machado's image of the soul as a garden, his own years in London pubs).
zitate_kontext: Leven on Doll by Doll between punk and rock.

1995-04-26-arbeiderbladet-mystisk-leven.kurz: Interview on the day of his concert at the Rockefeller, Oslo, as part of a “magical week” on the theme of healing.
inhalt: Interview on the day of his concert at the Rockefeller, Oslo, as part of a “magical week” on the theme of healing. The standfirst: the cult hero has quit drugs and turned to whisky production instead. On the album title, which Robert Bly tossed out on an occasion he hardly remembers, Leven says he has no clear idea what it means – what is mystic is the mystery itself. Sandnes recalls Doll by Doll and the silence after the attack, broken only by Mike Scott's cryptic thanks on *This Is the Sea* (Leven had let him “take the bus”).

Leven tells it soberly: after the attack he lost his voice, sat at home for a few years and took heroin; the silence led him back to a place he knew. His lyrics are about universal loneliness and the need to accept being alone; he likes to write about sadness, but “in a loving way”, and humour is the basis of life. He rejects being compared with Nick Drake, Syd Barrett or Kevin Ayers: he is neither dead nor a junkie nor mad, although he works with many mad people. He describes himself as a rough, tough, poetic guy. He started the whisky as a joke and then discovered the kinship of “spirit” and “sprit”.

1995-04-29-bergensavisen-bra-med-leven.kurz: Positive review of the solo concert at Garage on Thursday (27.04.1995): Leven can hold an audience alone with an acoustic guitar, you want to tie him down so he keeps playing; despite a break of almost twelve years he keeps up a high standard, and the voice makes the attack hard to believe.
inhalt: Positive review of the solo concert at Garage on Thursday (27.04.1995): Leven can hold an audience alone with an acoustic guitar, you want to tie him down so he keeps playing; despite a break of almost twelve years he keeps up a high standard, and the voice makes the attack hard to believe. Praise goes to his guitar playing (amplified by the sound engineer with a lot of reverb), the chat between songs with coarse stories from the drug years that audience and Leven laughed about, and, as the first encore, Van Morrison's “Slim Slow Slider”. The reviewer arrived a little late. Photo caption: no kilt, but the socks were in place.

1995-05-03-fremtiden-jackie-leven-rockef.titel: [Concert report with interview: Jackie Leven at the Rockefeller, Oslo]
1995-05-03-fremtiden-jackie-leven-rockef.kurz: Report on the solo concert in the “magical week” at the Rockefeller, Oslo – according to Andreassen Leven's first visit to Norway in over ten years.
inhalt: Report on the solo concert in the “magical week” at the Rockefeller, Oslo – according to Andreassen Leven's first visit to Norway in over ten years. Only Fremtiden and the rock magazine *Beat* were on the guest list; a small, enthusiastic audience would not let Leven leave the stage. Alone with a guitar, he had the audience holding their breath with pleasure; pieces from *The Mystery of Love* (including “Call Mother a Lonely Field”) and from the forthcoming album *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West*, due out in August, were played.

In conversation after the show Leven says he feels at home in Norway, although his last stay, in a band “with Glen Matlock, among others”, was not a happy time. As chairman of a London centre for people addicted to everything from sex to money, he believes in healing and acupuncture – for himself it is probably too late. On the new album: he asked Van Morrison to read a poem by the Belfast poet Louis MacNeice, Andy White takes part; the album is assembled like a film from speeches, poems, noises and songs, the range greater than before. The title means that in the West there are forbidden things one does not talk about – the West is slowly dying.

1995-05-11-eye-weekly-the-wild-boy-at-re.kurz: Feature in the Toronto free culture paper on the North American release of *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death* (True North/MCA), based on a telephone interview with Leven in London.
inhalt: Feature in the Toronto free culture paper on the North American release of *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death* (True North/MCA), based on a telephone interview with Leven in London. Anderson frames the piece with his own scepticism towards Robert Bly's *Iron John* and introduces Leven as the British spokesman of the “Mytho-Poetic Men's Movement”. He calls Doll by Doll an unjustly overlooked band, best on *Remember* and *Gypsy Blood*. Leven tells the Oban story: after the attack, heroin and a break-up, a night drive through a snowstorm to the west coast, in a bar the invitation from a half-Scottish, half-Polish giant to an arm-wrestle, from which a lifelong friendship grew – for him a turning point in his life. The “Argyll Cycle” (15 songs on an album and two EPs in 1994) documents the dying of his younger, wild self; you have to be defeated and betrayed to know who you are (“ignominy” as “no name”). Leven distances himself sharply from commercial men's courses (the warrior is an archetype we live in) and defends Bly against the charge of misogyny. On the cover of “I Say A Little Prayer” he develops the idea of the “black woman in you” for whom Bacharach/David wrote. Tone: very positive, compares the album with *Fisherman's Blues*.
zitate_kontext: Leven on his youth and Doll by Doll.

1995-09-28-moss-dagblad-forbidden-songs-.titel: [Record review: Jackie Leven – Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West]
1995-09-28-moss-dagblad-forbidden-songs-.kurz: Short review: the former Doll by Doll singer presents a successor to the previous year's “pearl”; for the uninitiated Leven is a cross between Bryan Ferry and Van Morrison and proves once again what a good singer he is.
inhalt: Short review: the former Doll by Doll singer presents a successor to the previous year's “pearl”; for the uninitiated Leven is a cross between Bryan Ferry and Van Morrison and proves once again what a good singer he is. Most of the material is self-written, and again poems (James Wright, Emily Dickinson) are set to music. Benevolent.

1995-09-29-arbeiderbladet-liv-og-leven.kurz: Positive review: big boys who cry, mothers who took their own lives, but also blessed moments – the songs are about personal growth, the basic mood is not depressing but heart-warming, soothing, almost spiritual.
inhalt: Positive review: big boys who cry, mothers who took their own lives, but also blessed moments – the songs are about personal growth, the basic mood is not depressing but heart-warming, soothing, almost spiritual. “Men in Prison” is singled out, over 60 sacred male voices; three of the 16 tracks are recitations of poems by Emily Dickinson, James Wright and Louis MacNeice. Leven draws on Celtic tunes, spaghetti westerns and rock; with country, jazz and oldies rock he goes a little limp, but overall a fine successor.

1995-10-22-bergensavisen-lite-leven.kurz: Praising review despite an ironic headline (“little noise”): the album is doomed to be a critics' darling and will hardly sell much, but is gloriously melancholy, full of catchy melodies and free of pop clichés.
inhalt: Praising review despite an ironic headline (“little noise”): the album is doomed to be a critics' darling and will hardly sell much, but is gloriously melancholy, full of catchy melodies and free of pop clichés. Leven “steals with style” – you can hear Morricone, Chris Isaak, Big Country and Morrissey. The rating is not legible in the OCR.

1995-10-24-fredriksstad-blad-ujevn-leven.kurz: Reserved short review in the “Speilet” column: *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West* (Amigo) is a collection of atmospheric, slightly pompous songs, a three-part “concept album” with Ireland as its starting point.
inhalt: Reserved short review in the “Speilet” column: *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West* (Amigo) is a collection of atmospheric, slightly pompous songs, a three-part “concept album” with Ireland as its starting point. Leven has a soft, warm voice and there is a lot of good music, but some songs remain mere parentheses – on the whole fairly uneven.

1995-11-03-rolling-stone-de-auf-den-spur.medium: Rolling Stone (German edition), online archive rollingstone.de
1995-11-03-rolling-stone-de-auf-den-spur.kurz: Early German-language interview profile from the time of “Forbidden Songs of the Dying West” (1995), written by Doebeling, long-standing Leven champion at the German Rolling Stone, after a visit to Argyll at Loch Feochan.
inhalt: Early German-language interview profile from the time of “Forbidden Songs of the Dying West” (1995), written by Doebeling, long-standing Leven champion at the German Rolling Stone, after a visit to Argyll at Loch Feochan. The text begins with cultural criticism of the nineties music business, which Leven shares “meaningfully”, and describes him physically (short trousers, white knee socks, sturdy footwear; at 45 “gnarled like an old oak”). Leven explains why he moved to the west coast: the people there are straightforward and have Irish blood, whereas the Scandinavian-Protestant east coast of his origins suits him less (self-statement). He presents himself and keyboard player James Hallawell as Celts (Fife and the “Kingdom of Cornwall” respectively). Doebeling recounts the personal catastrophes up to addiction, the independent heroin withdrawal and the founding of the CORE Trust, as well as Leven's role in Robert Bly's men's movement; Leven tells of wilderness weekends with a hundred men, poetry, drumming and stories. Doebeling ironically declines an invitation to take part. At the end he praises Doll by Doll as a band “between all stools” and the new double album as a near-perfect realisation of Leven's vision, much more fully worked out than its predecessor. The whisky “Leven's Lament” is also mentioned. Tone: ironic and detached towards the men's esotericism, full of admiration for the music.

1995-hachette-guide-du-routard-ecosse.titel: Le Guide du routard: Écosse (editions 1996–1997 and 1999)

1995-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.titel: [Collected finds Nasjonalbiblioteket 1995: brief news items, announcements, listings]

1996-04-26-the-independent-man-trouble.kurz: Early profile from the first Cooking Vinyl decade. Paul Du Noyer visits Leven at the CORE Trust near the Marylebone Road, where a portrait of the Princess of Wales hangs in reception, and introduces the former “psyche-punk” singer as co-founder of the addiction charity and British spokesman of Robert Bly's Men's Movement.
inhalt: Early profile from the first Cooking Vinyl decade. Paul Du Noyer visits Leven at the CORE Trust near the Marylebone Road, where a portrait of the Princess of Wales hangs in reception, and introduces the former “psyche-punk” singer as co-founder of the addiction charity and British spokesman of Robert Bly's Men's Movement. Leven wears knickerbockers and is a hard-drinking Scot. The attack of 1983, the end of Doll by Doll and the story of the girlfriend who ran off with the Dalai Lama's bodyguard and left Leven Bly cassettes are recounted. Leven defends the Men's Movement as common sense without a guru, speaks of “endarkenment” as the counterpart to enlightenment, promotes his whisky “Leven's Lament” (reportedly sold at Selfridges and Harrods) and bars as places of reflection. On the CORE Trust: no compulsory abstinence as in twelve-step programmes; ten staff, 30 therapists, supporters such as John Paul Getty Jr., Genesis, the Pet Shop Boys and Eric Clapton; Mike Scott donated a library. Musically current: The Argyll Cycle Volume One, with an album “Fairy Tales for Hard Men” planned.
zitate_kontext: Leven on spirituality in the therapy scene.

1996-05-02-haugesunds-avis-terapeutisk-j.kurz: Conversation held in Oslo by the NTB/Arbeiderbladet critic Haakon Larsen on the occasion of *The Argyll Cycle Vol.
inhalt: Conversation held in Oslo by the NTB/Arbeiderbladet critic Haakon Larsen on the occasion of *The Argyll Cycle Vol. 1*. Larsen opens by telling the familiar story – the stranglehold 13 years ago, heroin addiction, the woman who disappeared with the Dalai Lama's bodyguard, the return to Scotland. According to the article, the album's twelve songs all date from the second half of the 1980s; four of them were already on the two previous albums. The rest would have remained unreleased without pressure from fans who wanted to hear more from his convalescence; a second and final part is expected for the end of 1997.

Leven himself says that songwriting served him as therapy at the time; he sees himself more as a soul singer, “soulful” fits better than “spiritual” because his music is mostly sad – there is strength in sharing the experience of melancholy. Larsen describes him as calm and composed, praises his melodies and the “most graceful crooner voice this side of Scott Walker”, and thinks buyers of Van Morrison or Mark Knopfler might like him. The first album from 1971 and Doll by Doll as a “new wave” band from 1979 are mentioned.

The CORE Trust is described as a London foundation that works with acupuncture, poetry, music and rhythmics and is (according to the article) financed by Eric Clapton, Pete Townshend and other rock greats. At the time of the article Leven was in Bergen to lead a songwriting course for local musicians and to appear at the Ole Blues festival as the finale of a shorter Norwegian tour with the Irish troubadour Andy White.

1996-05-03-arbeiderbladet-mer-snadder.kurz: Positive short review: *The Argyll Cycle* is conceived as a two-record set, all songs written in Scotland, where Leven lived 1985–90 after his heroin period; some pieces have already been released.
inhalt: Positive short review: *The Argyll Cycle* is conceived as a two-record set, all songs written in Scotland, where Leven lived 1985–90 after his heroin period; some pieces have already been released. The twelve tracks are throughout brilliant songs by a professional, built on acoustic guitar and seasoned with band, saxophone, violin, mandolin, pedal steel and keyboards, with wistful melodies. Conclusion: another beautiful record by a songwriter who deserves his breakthrough.

1996-05-04-bergensavisen-leven-pa-verfte.titel: [Conversation with Jackie Leven at Verftet, Bergen]

1996-05-09-fremtiden-jackie-leven-kom-ti.kurz: Double page by the Fremtiden music journalist Johnny Andreassen, who had already conducted the interview with Leven in 1995.
inhalt: Double page by the Fremtiden music journalist Johnny Andreassen, who had already conducted the interview with Leven in 1995. Leven is back in Norway; last time only Fremtiden readers got to know him better, this time he visited all the big cities and appeared on the NRK1 Friday programme from Tromsø. Andreassen repeats Leven's earlier statement that he learned to speak and sing again with the Alexander Technique and that his voice is now better and stronger than ever.

Under the subheading “En kveld i magiens tegn” he describes the concert at the venue Rebekka West, Oslo: a good-humoured Leven alone with a guitar, a stomp board on which he beats time with his foot, and his voice; plus hours full of funny stories and songs of the last two or three years. One of them, told by Leven on stage: in a London restaurant he saw the football manager Terry Venables at the other end of the room; a note he wrote and an Indian waiter who did not understand English led to an angry Venables – a punchline story that Leven evidently used as a stage number.

The profile section sums up Doll by Doll (late 1970s on London club stages, white soul, Celtic and rock elements, in 1978 the hottest thing on the scene), the attack in 1982 after a studio session (three years without a voice, depression, heroin) and The Core Trust; the latter treats addictions of all kinds (alcohol, drugs, sex, money) with acupuncture and healing, and even the Queen has visited the centre. Leven released three albums in one year and announces more; his bond with Norway has grown stronger (subheading “Bånd til Norge”).

1996-05-11-harstad-tidende-en-juvel.kurz: Hymnic review: an album that captivates from the first moment, a masterpiece without a weak melody, “only pearls”; it even surpasses *The Mystery of Love*.
inhalt: Hymnic review: an album that captivates from the first moment, a masterpiece without a weak melody, “only pearls”; it even surpasses *The Mystery of Love*. Praise goes to the dark, crystal-clear voice, opulent but never pompous arrangements and the Scottish roots felt in the background; classic, acoustically anchored pop that you become addicted to. Short CV with Doll by Doll and *Grand Passion* (1982).

1996-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.titel: [Collected finds Nasjonalbiblioteket 1996: brief news items, announcements, listings]

1996-natt-og-dag-the-argyll-cycle.kurz: Review in the Oslo city magazine: in the mid-1980s Doll by Doll had a small, enthusiastic Norwegian following, and *Grand Passion* was the high point.
inhalt: Review in the Oslo city magazine: in the mid-1980s Doll by Doll had a small, enthusiastic Norwegian following, and *Grand Passion* was the high point. After whisky and heroin Leven is back, “the grand passion” still on the agenda. With a distinctive, romantic voice, melancholy songs and lush moods he is a man Norwegians like; at times it borders on pompous humbug, but it touches something in the sentimental Nordic.

1997-03-record-collector-jackie-leven-in.medium: Record Collector (interview for the magazine; transcript on Leven's website)
1997-03-record-collector-jackie-leven-in.kurz: Long conversation over Guinness on the eve of Leven's debut at the Royal Festival Hall as support for Bruce Cockburn (March 1997), shortly before *Fairytales For Hardmen*.
inhalt: Long conversation over Guinness on the eve of Leven's debut at the Royal Festival Hall as support for Bruce Cockburn (March 1997), shortly before *Fairytales For Hardmen*. Leven says the pseudonym (Sir) John St. Field came about when he was stopped by the police in the street and spontaneously assumed another identity; as St. Field he opened in the early 70s for ELO, Man, Quintessence, East of Eden and Colosseum II. *Control* was recorded in 1971/72 at Mayfair Studios and released only in Spain. He mentions a duo “Saint Judas” with Colin Soutar and a BBC session from Newcastle in 1969, as well as Walkman recordings from Greece (material for later Haunted Valley CDs). On Doll by Doll: the concert with U2 at the Venue in 1979 (he says he delivered a drunken monologue to U2), no live recordings, the recording of *Grand Passion* and of the unreleased *A Last Flick Of The Golden Wrench* in parallel in both Utopia studios with Tom Newman, the rights situation of the Automatic albums at Warner and a planned box set at Cooking Vinyl. He corrects the story of the attack himself: not his throat cut, but almost strangled, and not two years but “a year and a bit” without a voice; at the time he was living behind a fish-and-chip shop in Lisson Grove. Further: the genesis of *Fairytales* from two B-sides (“Poortoun”, “Sir Patrick Spens”), a planned live album at the 12 Bar Club, *Argyll Cycle Vol. 2* (with the Hilliard Ensemble?), the Argyll songs as the conclusion of a separation after which his ex-partner gave him Bly cassettes, the path to Cooking Vinyl (Sony interest, the lawyer's advice) and traditionals (Dick Gaughan, “Jim o Windygates”).
zitate_kontext: Leven on the time without a voice.

1997-04-02-glamdalen-leven-rolf-jacobsen.titel: [Jackie Leven and Rolf Jacobsen's «Solsikke» – Fairy Tales for Hard Men]
1997-04-02-glamdalen-leven-rolf-jacobsen.kurz: Music column reviewing the new album from the Rolf Jacobsen angle: Jacobsen's “Solsikke” closes *Fairy Tales for Hard Men* in Robert Bly's almost literal translation “Sunflower”, recited over a discreet rhythm.
inhalt: Music column reviewing the new album from the Rolf Jacobsen angle: Jacobsen's “Solsikke” closes *Fairy Tales for Hard Men* in Robert Bly's almost literal translation “Sunflower”, recited over a discreet rhythm. Bly, son of Norwegian emigrants (family name after Bleie in Hardanger), once translated Olav H. Hauge and later Jacobsen. Alongside Jacobsen are James Wright (“Saint Judas” as a song) and W. B. Yeats; the real achievement is how Leven's own songs against the “violent man in us” join with the great names. The author praises courage, ambition and voice. At the end: Leven begins a solo tour the next day (03.04.) at Dixie in Oslo, with eight further stops until 12 April. Jan Saghaug (from Slåstad, Sør-Odal), who made Leven's internet pages, reports that Leven may come back in the autumn with Doll by Doll and regards Norway as his second home.

1997-04-03-arbeiderbladet-leven-i-levend.kurz: Major interview on the day the tour starts in Oslo. Leven says Robert Bly stays with him when he comes to Britain; then they sit up for a week exchanging poems and life experience, and every time Bly has his “Norwegian night” – that is how he came to appreciate Rolf Jacobsen.
inhalt: Major interview on the day the tour starts in Oslo. Leven says Robert Bly stays with him when he comes to Britain; then they sit up for a week exchanging poems and life experience, and every time Bly has his “Norwegian night” – that is how he came to appreciate Rolf Jacobsen. “Sunflower” is a hard poem by any standard of manhood: we take things too personally, while an energy streams through the universe beside which one's own happiness is a trifle.

Asked about the closeness of his lyrics to depression and madness, Leven says he seeks the “freezing moment” that a good poem gives; on this record the images are clearer to him than ever before. Some, such as “Sad Polish Song”, are so strong that he cannot sing them on stage without being completely knocked over; Yeats and Jacobsen overcame themselves – that is his aim too.

Leven now wants to write more, including an autobiography, once his parents can no longer read it. To that end he stepped down as head of the centre for drug addicts: after eleven years with two full-time jobs, withdrawing is a relief, the staff are carrying on the ideas and concept, and *The Big Issue* wants to set up a similar facility in Glasgow. Announced are: a CD reissue of the Doll by Doll catalogue with a reunion tour, due to begin in August in Oslo and Bergen, a live record and a “sister album” to *Fairy Tales* entitled “Injured Women” – poems by women about women wounded in the soul, by his own account “hopefully my most miserable record”.

Steinkjer acknowledges the loyal Norwegian following since Doll by Doll and mentions the whisky Leven's Lament. On the album's second Norwegian reference, the thanks to the bar of the Grand Hotel in Tromsø, Leven says that on his last visit he spent a lot of time there working through a difficult question of life; the bar is a peaceful reminder of a world he is afraid of. He openly admits that he sometimes wishes he were not alive.

1997-04-04-arbeiderbladet-ikke-lett-a-va.kurz: Positive review: after the lost years of intoxication Leven has a lot to say; titles such as “Boy Trapped in a Man”, “Extremely Violent Man”, “Fear of Women” and “Sexual Danger” show that he is wrestling with the male role.
inhalt: Positive review: after the lost years of intoxication Leven has a lot to say; titles such as “Boy Trapped in a Man”, “Extremely Violent Man”, “Fear of Women” and “Sexual Danger” show that he is wrestling with the male role. Music Celtic in its roots, expressive melodies; quotations from “Yesterday” and “Unchained Melody” fit in, the three pieces with Doll by Doll do not stand out particularly. Praise goes to the poetic sense: Yeats' “Mad as the Mist and Snow” set to music, and at the end Jacobsen's “Solsikke” in Bly's translation as a worthy conclusion.

1997-04-04-nordlys-fairy-tales-for-hard-.kurz: Benevolent review with a rating of 5 (out of 6): Leven has learned from his mistakes, and on the album a “knowing man” speaks in small novellas about subjects men hardly talk about, without a raised finger or sentimentality.
inhalt: Benevolent review with a rating of 5 (out of 6): Leven has learned from his mistakes, and on the album a “knowing man” speaks in small novellas about subjects men hardly talk about, without a raised finger or sentimentality. The album is demanding – because of the content, the Scottish-tinged English and the “crushing” sound samples. The highlight is “Old West African Song” (text of unknown origin) with African rhythms and Scottish tones; Jacobsen's poem sounds only with percussion. A note on the concert at Blå Rock on Sunday (06.04.).
zitate_kontext: with a view to the Tromsø concert.

1997-04-08-nordlys-ikke-bare-for-harde-m.kurz: Enthusiastic review of the night concert (23:00–2:00) at Blå Rock Café on 06.04.1997 in front of about a hundred listeners: Leven on a stool next to the jukebox, guitar and stamping foot as percussion, guitar playing reaching as far as hints of flamenco.
inhalt: Enthusiastic review of the night concert (23:00–2:00) at Blå Rock Café on 06.04.1997 in front of about a hundred listeners: Leven on a stool next to the jukebox, guitar and stamping foot as percussion, guitar playing reaching as far as hints of flamenco. Between songs he told “fairy tales for adults” – about what hard men don't do (talk to their children), self-mockingly about the girlfriend who left him for the Dalai Lama's bodyguard, later coarser stories about whisky, pizza and sex. He talked with the audience, not just to it.

1997-04-09-bergensavisen-eventyr-for-har.kurz: Positive review that starts from the cover (Peter Howson's painting “The Bodybuilder”): a hard man who wants respect from men and love from a woman who never comes.
inhalt: Positive review that starts from the cover (Peter Howson's painting “The Bodybuilder”): a hard man who wants respect from men and love from a woman who never comes. Leven quotes his formula of boys trapped in men's lives and playing men; the inspiration is again Robert Bly (“Iron John”, 1990). Despite the titles, it is above all a poetic, beautiful record with Celtic roots; “Poortoun” is “downright picture-perfect”, Doll by Doll play on a few tracks. A warning against repetition given such high productivity; a side-swipe at the failed Norwegian government committee on the male role.

1997-04-09-nordlandsposten-leven-for-bod.titel: [Interview before the Bodø concert: «Dere kan vente en veldig loud Scotsman»]
1997-04-09-nordlandsposten-leven-for-bod.kurz: Preliminary interview ahead of the first Bodø concert (Den Siste Glæde, Sunday 13.04.1997) on the music page, alongside a short review of *Fairytales for Hard Men* (“folksanger i stor-format”: raw, hard and yet warm and humorous; you need strong nerves to take the whole album in one go).
inhalt: Preliminary interview ahead of the first Bodø concert (Den Siste Glæde, Sunday 13.04.1997) on the music page, alongside a short review of *Fairytales for Hard Men* (“folksanger i stor-format”: raw, hard and yet warm and humorous; you need strong nerves to take the whole album in one go).

Leven announces that the audience can expect a very “loud” Scotsman with a loud guitar and sad rock songs, plus funny stories. The biggest problem when playing solo, he says, is the audience's beer consumption; but his guitar makes enough noise, and he even plays drum solos on it. Doll by Doll played on three tracks of the new album; in the autumn they intended to reissue the old albums and do a small Norwegian tour. Norway, he says, is the country he values most after Scotland. He has already been to Tromsø and thanks the bar in the Grand Hotel on the sleeve; during a stopover in Bodø the previous year he had decided to ask his Norwegian tour manager for a gig there.

He has only good things to say about Mike Scott, with whom he worked on his first solo album. He got to know Rolf Jacobsen through Robert Bly, who translated “Solsikke” for him; with Bly he occasionally holds poetry evenings at which a lot of Jacobsen is read. He hears for the first time of Henning Gravrok from Bodø, who has made a whole album of Jacobsen texts, and would like to meet him. At the end he asks about Bodø; asked about salmon, he says wild salmon is good anywhere, but he rejects farmed salmon – and reacts drastically when he hears that Ian Anderson (Jethro Tull) runs a salmon farm.

1997-04-12-bergensavisen-historiefortell.kurz: Positive review of the solo concert at a well-attended Garage on Thursday (10.04.1997): Leven sits on a monitor rather than on the chair and, between poetic minor-key ballads, tells coarse, at times hysterically funny stories; the recurring themes are boys who become hard men, images from the Scottish Highlands and love under poor conditions. Played were, among others, “Stranger on the Square” and “Young Male Suicide Blessed by Invisible Woman”. Leven remarks that the audience is much quieter than last time; he announces his return with Doll by Doll in late summer and names the sister album “Injured Women: The Jackie Leven Report”.
inhalt: Positive review of the solo concert at a well-attended Garage on Thursday (10.04.1997): Leven sits on a monitor rather than on the chair and, between poetic minor-key ballads, tells coarse, at times hysterically funny stories; the recurring themes are boys who become hard men, images from the Scottish Highlands and love under poor conditions. Played were, among others, “Stranger on the Square” and “Young Male Suicide Blessed by Invisible Woman”. Leven remarks that the audience is much quieter than last time; he announces his return with Doll by Doll in late summer and names the sister album “Injured Women: The Jackie Leven Report”.

1997-04-14-lofotposten-hvit-manns-soul.kurz: Very positive review of the concert at Præstengbrygga, Kabelvåg, on Saturday (12.04.1997) before around 120 guests, of whom, by the author's estimate, only about 20 had known Leven beforehand.
inhalt: Very positive review of the concert at Præstengbrygga, Kabelvåg, on Saturday (12.04.1997) before around 120 guests, of whom, by the author's estimate, only about 20 had known Leven beforehand. He began around 11 pm with a story about homesickness and building fences in the rain on a farm in the north of England, followed by “Farm Boy”; further songs included “Peace Comes Dropping Slow”. Self-mocking, at times bizarre stories – by his own account he had been a bastard – contrasted with deadly serious songs; guitar and shoe soles as rhythm. Two hours without an interval; Leven found many things in common with Scotland and promised to return soon.

1997-04-14-troms-folkeblad-ekte-vare-fra.kurz: Mixed-to-positive review of the two-hour solo concert at Sumaloftet, Finnsnes, on Friday (11.04.1997) before a good hundred listeners; Leven opened with a coarse joke.
inhalt: Mixed-to-positive review of the two-hour solo concert at Sumaloftet, Finnsnes, on Friday (11.04.1997) before a good hundred listeners; Leven opened with a coarse joke. Honesty and humility carried the in itself “stillborn” concept of man-with-guitar; the songs were simply built, the sound not very varied until it improved towards the end. The critic would have liked accordion, fiddle, flute or harmonica; verdict: a pleasant acquaintance.

1997-04-15-nordlands-framtid-en-poetisk-.kurz: Positive review of Leven's first concert in Bodø (Den Siste Glæde, Sunday 13.04.1997, around 150 listeners, just under two hours).
inhalt: Positive review of Leven's first concert in Bodø (Den Siste Glæde, Sunday 13.04.1997, around 150 listeners, just under two hours). He began with “Farm Boy” and the prison story “Shadow in My Eye” from the debut. The stories about beer, whisky and sex were told so casually and decadently that he did not come across as a “dirty old man” but as disarmingly funny; more important, however, was the music: guitar as both guitar and drum, left foot as rhythm machine, voice like a “soulful Highland horn”. Leven, the reviewer says, has gone from critics' darling to audience favourite.

1997-04-15-nordlandsposten-leven-pa-glae.kurz: Mostly positive review of the same Bodø concert (13.04.1997, a good 150 visitors): reflective and atmospheric, solo with acoustic guitar, most songs from the new album; Leven in the Dylan songwriter tradition, but with a form of his own (sitar-like guitar turns, drum solos on the body of the guitar, throaty singing, a whistled western theme à la Sergio Leone – unfortunately in at least three songs). In the middle of the set one of the most beautiful ballads the venue has heard; at times long-winded. Stage patter: he could go back to the hotel for the porn channel, wanted to open “Jackie Leven's Scottish Bastard Pub” in Bodø; plus a minibar anecdote from Hamburg. At the end he threatened to come back next year.
inhalt: Mostly positive review of the same Bodø concert (13.04.1997, a good 150 visitors): reflective and atmospheric, solo with acoustic guitar, most songs from the new album; Leven in the Dylan songwriter tradition, but with a form of his own (sitar-like guitar turns, drum solos on the body of the guitar, throaty singing, a whistled western theme à la Sergio Leone – unfortunately in at least three songs). In the middle of the set one of the most beautiful ballads the venue has heard; at times long-winded. Stage patter: he could go back to the hotel for the porn channel, wanted to open “Jackie Leven's Scottish Bastard Pub” in Bodø; plus a minibar anecdote from Hamburg. At the end he threatened to come back next year.

1997-05-03-firda-eventyr-fra-jackie-leve.kurz: Lukewarm review in Nynorsk: fairy tales played a greater role in pre-Christian times; Leven tells of men and women who are supposed to emulate hard role models and combines this with pretty, melancholy folk-rock tones.
inhalt: Lukewarm review in Nynorsk: fairy tales played a greater role in pre-Christian times; Leven tells of men and women who are supposed to emulate hard role models and combines this with pretty, melancholy folk-rock tones. Beautiful and melodious throughout, but nothing that stands out from the average; guitar and voice carry one “in a perfectly okay way” through the 16 tracks.

1997-06-q-bawdy-jackie-leven-shocks-scan.kurz: Report on Leven's solo concert at the basement club Garage in Bergen on 10.04.1997, combined with quotations from conversation.
inhalt: Report on Leven's solo concert at the basement club Garage in Bergen on 10.04.1997, combined with quotations from conversation. Aizlewood describes the coarse stage stories with which Leven introduces songs such as “In The Greenwood”, and notes a changed Leven: slimmer, better dressed, country life in Hampshire with Deborah Greenwood, reduced commitments at the CORE Trust. Leven calls his career “spectacularly unsuccessful” and openly admits two legends to be a “scam”: the whisky “Leven's Lament” was only a small bottling of a respected whisky, and Bob Dylan's co-authorship of “As We Sailed Into Skibbereen” after a shared train journey was invented. Bergen, where Leven allegedly played his first professional gigs in 1966, had taken *Fairytales For Hardmen* to number 40 in the Norwegian charts. Two hours solo, no encores, with requests from the audience; “Marble City Bar” is about a suicide attempt in Ireland, “Desolation Blues” is dedicated to the late Q writer John Bauldie. Leven announces a return with the reunited Doll by Doll in the same year and the album *Injured Women: The Leven Report*, and talks about lost self-esteem since his heroin addiction. Tone: amused and admiring.

1997-08-31-bergensavisen-dukker-i-fint-d.kurz: Positive review of the first Doll by Doll concert in 15 years at the basement club Garage: Leven joked that they were four “living dolls”; the band “came into its own”, cheers at every little gesture, Leven with a plastic beer cup.
inhalt: Positive review of the first Doll by Doll concert in 15 years at the basement club Garage: Leven joked that they were four “living dolls”; the band “came into its own”, cheers at every little gesture, Leven with a plastic beer cup. Quality and intimacy were right: in quiet pieces an almost reverent mood, otherwise drive; fruitful guitar dialogues between Leven and Joe Shaw, solid to brilliant bass from Kevin Foster, power from drummer David McIntosh (“McIntern” in the paper). The band appears in hardly any rock history book and was never big, but for its fans it is more than good enough.

1997-10-25-drammens-tidende-fram-fra-ska.kurz: Short review of the CD edition of *Control* as a “funny curiosity” for the many who have meanwhile become attached to the Celtic soul of Leven and Doll by Doll.
inhalt: Short review of the CD edition of *Control* as a “funny curiosity” for the many who have meanwhile become attached to the Celtic soul of Leven and Doll by Doll. According to the article, the album was recorded “as early as 1966” by a young Scot on the run from the law; Leven writes in the booklet that he was completely on LSD at the time and that the record came out only briefly in Spain in 1973. One hears the same voice and the same soulful melodic construction, but not the great experience of the later albums. Also: in 1969 Leven boarded a ship to Bergen – his first trip abroad – hence his special relationship with Norway.

1997-12-wavelength-jackie-leven-ulrich-b.kurz: Interview by the German Van Morrison fan Ulrich Begemeier for the British Van Morrison newsletter, conducted on 22.09.1997 at the Sinkkasten in Frankfurt am Main (Morrison once played there as “Storyville” with the Monarchs).
inhalt: Interview by the German Van Morrison fan Ulrich Begemeier for the British Van Morrison newsletter, conducted on 22.09.1997 at the Sinkkasten in Frankfurt am Main (Morrison once played there as “Storyville” with the Monarchs). Leven talks about the reissue of *Control* (LSD imagery), the pseudonym John St. Field (trouble with the police in a northern English town), years in Madrid, Berlin, South America and Dorset, Doll by Doll falling between two stools (like The Yachts, The Original Mirrors, The Only Ones), unreleased Virgin recordings, the attack, heroin and the CORE Trust, which he said he had handed over to his friend Jason Wright but remains a “father-figure”. He reports on the Doll by Doll concert in Brussels with Jo Shaw and David McIntosh (Shaw is currently building a studio for George Martin), on a song not used for the film *Sid & Nancy*, and on having received the German critics' annual prize in Bonn the day before (after a journey from Bautzen via Hannover, Hamburg and Düsseldorf), where he sang “The Bonnie Earl O' Moray” unaccompanied. A large part concerns Van Morrison: “Slim Slow Slider” on *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow*, “Hungry For Your Love”, Hillman's term “pathos”, *Veedon Fleece* as favourite album, being neighbours in Notting Hill, the 1995 Q Awards. Plans: Doll by Doll CDs, Charisma/Virgin material, *Argyll Cycle Vol. II*, *Injured Women*, an album setting Russian poetry to music (Mandelstam, Akhmatova). At the end he explains the Artaud photo on the covers.
zitate_kontext: Leven on Van Morrison's song imagery.

1997-clearspot-jackie-leven-tower-arts-c.kurz: Enthusiastic report on a solo concert in the small, sold-out Tower Theatre in Winchester at the time of *Fairytales For Hardmen*.
inhalt: Enthusiastic report on a solo concert in the small, sold-out Tower Theatre in Winchester at the time of *Fairytales For Hardmen*. Plumbley celebrates Leven as a Celtic bard and storyteller, describes the percussive guitar playing (the guitar, a Gallagher, once belonged to Doc Watson, according to Leven) and relays Leven's Clapton anecdote (Clapton listens during the recording of “Call Mother A Lonely Field” and afterwards only wants to show off his coat). Leven refuses encore rituals, takes requests, reads forgotten lyrics from a fan's CD booklet and, at the insistence of the Doll by Doll fans in the front row, plays “Main Travelled Roads”. With the complete setlist (19 titles, from “Farm Boy” to “Gylen Gylen”).

1997-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.titel: [Collected finds Nasjonalbiblioteket 1997: brief news items, announcements, listings]

1998-03-06-nordlys-live-med-leven.kurz: Half-page portrait ahead of Leven's tour of northern Norway in March 1998, largely assembled from British interviews (Q, Mojo) and memories of the Tromsø concert in 1997.
inhalt: Half-page portrait ahead of Leven's tour of northern Norway in March 1998, largely assembled from British interviews (Q, Mojo) and memories of the Tromsø concert in 1997. Emberland begins with the image of the man with his own whisky, his own detox clinic, men's work and “more and coarser bawdy jokes than an entire Rorbua clientele”, and recapitulates the legend: start as John St. Field, “punk band” Doll by Doll, a choking attack in a side street in north London, heroin, the girlfriend who vanished with the Dalai Lama's bodyguard, then the “CORE Thrust college” with (alleged) support from Princess Diana.

On the whisky Leven's Lament he quotes Leven's stage joke from 1997 (the crate of samples disappeared at Fornebu airport) and – from Q – the admission that the whisky was bottled by his favourite brand and merely relabelled; after all, you can also have “Sting cognac and Tina Turner chardonnay”. Leven is a great fibber, but an even greater storyteller. Further: Leven as a kind of English branch of Robert Bly's men's movement; his own statements on *Fairy Tales* (fairy tales as stories for everyone, men who are mostly still boys, the “impoverished woman” in men) and a coarse stage anecdote from Tromsø 1997 about his partner Deborah. From Mojo: he loves telling fragmented stories on stage and seeing when people are really moved; from Q: heroin cost him a lot of self-confidence and he needs reassurance that he has not messed it up.

Outlook: Doll by Doll are slowly reuniting; in a month Leven goes into the studio for “Injured Women – The Leven Report”, due in the autumn, together with a Doll by Doll box of six albums including the unreleased “Last Flick of the Golden Wrench” and a regular best-of. Tour dates in the box: Huset, Hammerfest (Wednesday), Blå Rock Café, Tromsø (Thursday), Præstengbrygga, Kabelvåg (Saturday).

1998-03-12-nordlys-fin-by-a-vaere-ensom-.kurz: Conversation on the day of the concert in Tromsø (his third appearance there within two years). Leven says Tromsø is a beautiful city in which to be lonely; loneliness is one of his themes.
inhalt: Conversation on the day of the concert in Tromsø (his third appearance there within two years). Leven says Tromsø is a beautiful city in which to be lonely; loneliness is one of his themes. He does not want to be called a poet: that is a title others bestow on you, and it frightens him when young people wake up one morning and think of themselves as poets – you can write well without being a poet (with a coarse comparison). He gets ideas from small observations, such as the way an old woman turns round in the street. The song “Burning the Box of Beautiful Things” was partly written in the bar of the Grand Hotel: the barmaid's reaction to a situation gave him the third verse. He writes constantly, even when he was at rock bottom; in the evening he wants to play some new songs for the first time.

1998-03-16-lofotposten-leven-for-dove-or.kurz: A panning of the audience, not of the artist: at the second Kabelvåg concert (Præstengbrygga, Saturday 14.03.1998) the great majority had come to talk.
inhalt: A panning of the audience, not of the artist: at the second Kabelvåg concert (Præstengbrygga, Saturday 14.03.1998) the great majority had come to talk. Leven tried to drown out the chatterers, grew irritated and asked them to shut up, whereupon the audience responded with an even more annoying chorus of shushing. Leven got his job done with voice and guitar, but the joy and fire disappeared, and the stories that had spiced the “excellent” concert of April 1997 were missing entirely. For the reviewer the evening was “totally ruined”; he hopes Leven will not skip Kabelvåg next time.

1998-04-25-yahoo-groups-leven-mailinglis.kurz: The group describes itself as a mailing list about the “life, work and times” of Jackie Leven, his artistic influences, his earlier work as John St. Field and with Doll by Doll; it spreads news about concerts and records and permits a “limited exchange of mp3's” in the “Files” section.
inhalt: The group describes itself as a mailing list about the “life, work and times” of Jackie Leven, his artistic influences, his earlier work as John St. Field and with Doll by Doll; it spreads news about concerts and records and permits a “limited exchange of mp3's” in the “Files” section. As a further address it gives www.jackieleven.com. In 2001/2002 it was open and unmoderated, in February 2003 “restricted membership”; the message archive was always accessible to members only.

The Yahoo archive begins in September 2000 (147 messages, October 347, November 201, December 214). In 2001 the monthly figures ranged between 103 and 290 (total for 2001: around 2,200), in 2002 between 50 and 230, in January/February 2003 at 284 and 311 – that is, roughly 3 to 10 messages a day. The message numbers stand at about 1070 in February 2001 and about 1470 in April 2001.

1998-07-rip-it-up-jackie-leven-robert-du.kurz: Preview of Leven's first Australian tour (July 1998) with a telephone interview. Leven looks forward to the country, holds out the prospect of a return with his band The Celtic Soul Men to the Womadelaide festival in February, and explains his greater popularity in Europe by saying that he went to Berlin, Madrid and South America when young and lost touch with Britain.
inhalt: Preview of Leven's first Australian tour (July 1998) with a telephone interview. Leven looks forward to the country, holds out the prospect of a return with his band The Celtic Soul Men to the Womadelaide festival in February, and explains his greater popularity in Europe by saying that he went to Berlin, Madrid and South America when young and lost touch with Britain. Dunstan quotes the blurb of the Cooking Vinyl sampler *Cooking Rhythms* (with an alleged Salman Rushdie quotation about the whisky Leven's Lament) and reports that Cooking Vinyl is planning a Doll by Doll box with the working title “Swimming In A Lonely Pool”; Leven is considering an album of Tim Hardin songs. He is bringing *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow* and EPs and announces material from the just-finished *Night Lilies*. Closing concert: Governor Hindmarsh, Adelaide, Thu. 30 July (1998).

1998-09-07-bergensavisen-whiskyen-pa-hyl.kurz: Interview on the release of *Night Lilies* (mistakenly “Night Lines” in the standfirst), which Leven describes as emotional songs in a rocky wrapping.
inhalt: Interview on the release of *Night Lilies* (mistakenly “Night Lines” in the standfirst), which Leven describes as emotional songs in a rocky wrapping. He wanted to trace how a particular smell, sound or movement triggers intense memories of very specific episodes. The album is less melancholy than *Fairy Tales*: the colours still dark, but clearer; the aim is a sad record that at the same time lifts you up. Nothing does him as much good as walking the streets and watching people – in the past he did not do that.

Guitarist Joe Shaw from the Doll by Doll days plays on the album. Leven: Joe has always been a good friend, but the band years were traumatic in many respects; nobody liked them, they themselves were convinced of their class and sometimes took a perverse pleasure in flattening the audience with an overwhelmingly heavy live show until the hostility became palpable. Today he can laugh about it and is proud of the records. Releasing the climax of a song is like wrestling with an angel.

On the whisky Leven's Lament he says that, ironically, he no longer likes whisky: after a bout of nausea he has to turn away at the mere smell – bad advertising, as the “workers” pointed out to him. Halleraker recalls that at earlier Bergen gigs Leven talked more than he played; Leven: friends call him a lying bastard, but he likes inventing little stories that put the big things in perspective. Announcement: Garage, 30 October 1998, “one of his hardest rock concerts in a long time”.

1998-09-08-dagsavisen-mye-liv-i-leven.kurz: Leven has become a kind of “Norgesvenn”; he is releasing his fourth album in four years and is coming in October with a full band for the first time.
inhalt: Leven has become a kind of “Norgesvenn”; he is releasing his fourth album in four years and is coming in October with a full band for the first time. The songs “just poured out of him”; four albums, singles, EPs and a lot of touring have made him known above all in Germany and Norway. Nilsen summarises Doll by Doll (critically acclaimed “post-punk” band, silence after *Grand Passion* in 1982), the legend of the girlfriend, the choking attack and heroin, and the comeback in 1994. Leven laughs: apart from his “accidents”, it was wonderful to do nothing for years; all he ever had to do was live and observe – but when the songs came, he had to write them down, record them and play them.

*Night Lilies* is about memories and the tricks memory plays. On Robert Bly and the “Men's Movement”, Leven says Bly has sensible things to say about men and women. The hardest thing he has experienced was the break-up with his girlfriend two years ago because he had fallen in love with another woman; today he lives on the Scottish west coast with his new partner and her children. He wants to process this chapter on “Injured Women: The Leven Report”, which is meant to show that he does not write only about masculinity. Planned: a 6-CD box with Doll by Doll's complete work including the unreleased fifth album, and next year a new, differently sounding, possibly more electronic album with new people.

Tour dates in the text: Stavanger (20.10.), Kabelvåg (21.), Bodø (22.), Trondheim (23.), Førde (24.), Oslo (29.), Bergen (30.10.1998). Leven: apart from the reunion concerts with Doll by Doll in Bergen the previous year, he has never brought a band to Norway.

1998-09-08-tonsbergs-blad-levende-minner.kurz: NTB Pluss interview conducted in Oslo on *Night Lilies*. The key words of the album are memory and remembrance: how with age one forgets and falsifies memories, until a smell, a taste or a sound suddenly brings them back.
inhalt: NTB Pluss interview conducted in Oslo on *Night Lilies*. The key words of the album are memory and remembrance: how with age one forgets and falsifies memories, until a smell, a taste or a sound suddenly brings them back. That is exactly what happened to him in the summer of 1997 on a small Greek island: the scent of a flower took him straight back to childhood and youth in Scotland and awakened forgotten memories, some of which ended up on the album; all eleven songs have a real basis, even if not all of them describe his own experiences.

On Doll by Doll Leven says the band deserved a better fate but had only itself to blame for never breaking through: so aggressive and unfriendly that it made many enemies; he himself was violent at the time and thought that was right because his friends were the same. He led a life on the edge, and ironically it was precisely the severe assault that saved him: for two years he could not speak, for six years he could not sing, but he had time to withdraw to Scotland and take stock of his life – he emerged from convalescence a better person. A great deal of energy afterwards went into the centre for homeless drug addicts that he founded. He has enjoyed telling stories since childhood and gives them a fitting mood; *Night Lilies* is considerably warmer than *Fairy Tales*. The ending (destroyed by OCR) mentions Rolf Jacobsen, plans to set more poems by his “good friend” and other poets to music on the next record, and the October tour.
zitate_kontext: Leven on the Doll by Doll years.

1998-09-11-jaerbladet-leven-ikke-leven-i.kurz: Youth-pages interview shortly before the release of *Night Lilies* (Monday 14.09.). Friestad gives Leven's place of residence as the small town of Titchfield between Southampton and Portsmouth.
inhalt: Youth-pages interview shortly before the release of *Night Lilies* (Monday 14.09.). Friestad gives Leven's place of residence as the small town of Titchfield between Southampton and Portsmouth. Leven on his release concert in Oslo in a small club for only 40 people: hard work, but good, people told him afterwards that the songs had made them cry. The album is about buried, partly painful memories that you only get rid of when you learn from them. He is self-taught, tunes and plays the guitar in his own way and “cannot play normally at all”; in the studio he is “quite military”, but open to suggestions. He thinks in images and then looks for words for them; his lyrics contain no humour, but “jokes”. Favourite song: “Burning the Box of Beautiful Things”. Appended is a short review (disappointing at first, then growing, “Celt/Soul” after Q).

1998-09-12-drammens-tidende-det-store-hj.kurz: Music page by Johnny Andreassen (formerly Fremtiden) with an interview on the sofa at the Hotel Savoy and a short review.
inhalt: Music page by Johnny Andreassen (formerly Fremtiden) with an interview on the sofa at the Hotel Savoy and a short review. Andreassen describes Leven as an artist who puts more soul and heart into it than anyone else he has met; Leven is slowly becoming prominent in Norway after frequent acoustic tours, and a Norwegian (Jan Saghaug) made his official website. At the last meeting the talk was of fairy tales for men and the ability to cry; at that time Leven announced an album about injustice towards women (“Injured Woman”). Now he says that, unfortunately, he has since hurt his partner again; something of what he wanted to say about women's fates is also in *Night Lilies*.

According to Leven, the album title goes back to large night lilies that grew in his youth along a disused railway line in a forbidden area and opened only late in the evening; at 16–17 he mostly brawled and drank. He forgot the flowers until he found them again late one evening on a remote Greek island – the scent hit him like a shock. He speaks of “memory chances” and warns that being open can destroy you (example Bill Clinton). On the whisky: Leven's Lament is still being produced but is hardly available, Harrods is said to be a safe source; in his youth one could choose between the paper mill, the coal mine and the whisky bottling plant, workers received eight bottles a week, and his home town had Europe's highest unemployment and the most suicides for three years. He no longer drinks whisky himself.

Announcement of the big Norwegian tour in October with Steafan Hannigan (Irish flutes, percussion) and Michael Cosgrave (keyboard, trumpet).
