The review calls *Night Lilies* a pearl with some of his most beautiful melodies and more experimental rock moods, “Celtic soul” with “perhaps the most beautiful male voice of our time”. A box quotes Leven's love of Gothic horror storytellers.
zitate_kontext: Leven (from the earlier conversation, as a headline quotation).

1998-09-16-dagsavisen-liv-og-leven.kurz: Very positive review: smell can evoke time and place even more strongly than music; Leven let himself be inspired by the scent of the night lilies, which by his own account shaped his life.
inhalt: Very positive review: smell can evoke time and place even more strongly than music; Leven let himself be inspired by the scent of the night lilies, which by his own account shaped his life. The album is hardly weaker than its predecessor, one of the highlights of 1997: unusually strong, painfully personal stories about the difficult relationship between women and men, melodies that seem familiar yet are entirely his own, an earthy Celtic mood and tasteful playing; at times he appears as “the Roy Orbison of our time”. Leven became big in small circles in Norway – that the previous album reached number 40 on a Norwegian sales list caused a stir in the British rock press – but remains one of the most underrated rock singers in the world. Caption: concert in Oslo on 29 October.

1998-09-18-glamdalen-liljedugg.kurz: Positive review: Leven, former singer of the “semi-legendary” Doll by Doll and ex-junkie, has fought his way back after “the biggest helping of bad luck in history”; *Fairy Tales* brought him deserved success.
inhalt: Positive review: Leven, former singer of the “semi-legendary” Doll by Doll and ex-junkie, has fought his way back after “the biggest helping of bad luck in history”; *Fairy Tales* brought him deserved success. *Night Lilies* is more conventional, but still “Caledonian Soul” from the same source as Van Morrison once drew on: pure as silver, fresh as morning dew, eleven carefully chiselled songs full of wisdom and hope, for anyone who has lost faith or wants to hear beautiful music.

1998-09-25-bergensavisen-night-lilies.kurz: Positive short review of the “Scottish friend of Bergen”: the title track opens, with a Dylan feel, a gloriously melancholy record in the line of the earlier solo albums; with his paws firmly in British folk music, Leven tells stories that cut through the skin, the airy atmosphere gives a cool dreamlike feeling, and he never provokes with boorishness. Music for late autumn evenings, preferably with Leven's own whisky in the glass, when you want to find out what went wrong – “Jackie Leven knows the answer”.
inhalt: Positive short review of the “Scottish friend of Bergen”: the title track opens, with a Dylan feel, a gloriously melancholy record in the line of the earlier solo albums; with his paws firmly in British folk music, Leven tells stories that cut through the skin, the airy atmosphere gives a cool dreamlike feeling, and he never provokes with boorishness. Music for late autumn evenings, preferably with Leven's own whisky in the glass, when you want to find out what went wrong – “Jackie Leven knows the answer”.

1998-10-02-helgelands-blad-night-lilies.kurz: Mixed review: Leven again wanders dark paths in the Scottish Highlands and makes of them melodious, poetic rock with folk elements, airily arranged and rich in detail; the themes are betrayal and lost or won love, this time with memories that catch up with you.
inhalt: Mixed review: Leven again wanders dark paths in the Scottish Highlands and makes of them melodious, poetic rock with folk elements, airily arranged and rich in detail; the themes are betrayal and lost or won love, this time with memories that catch up with you. Weakness: Leven can seem excessively pompous, with no sense of proportion in heartache, plus a tendency towards an overly velvety vocal register. Nevertheless worthwhile for friends of dramatic, romantic rock music.

1998-10-16-harstad-tidende-ujevnt-fra-ja.kurz: Slightly disappointed review by the same reviewer who had celebrated *The Argyll Cycle* in 1996: production gleaming, song material good, but signs of stagnation – where Leven previously renewed himself in details, this time it follows familiar paths too much, one constantly has the feeling of having heard it all before.
inhalt: Slightly disappointed review by the same reviewer who had celebrated *The Argyll Cycle* in 1996: production gleaming, song material good, but signs of stagnation – where Leven previously renewed himself in details, this time it follows familiar paths too much, one constantly has the feeling of having heard it all before. The highlight is the ballad “Empty in Soho Square”, in which Leven sings “most magically”. Verdict: disappoints somewhat, but worth buying.

1998-10-23-lofotposten-en-perfekt-kveld.kurz: Enthusiastic review of the third Kabelvåg concert (Præstengbrygga, Wednesday 21.10.1998, 80 listeners), written twelve hours afterwards.
inhalt: Enthusiastic review of the third Kabelvåg concert (Præstengbrygga, Wednesday 21.10.1998, 80 listeners), written twelve hours afterwards. Leven came up the stairs in the half-light shortly before 11 pm and, after the first song and the first anecdote, had the audience in his grip for two hours: gallows humour, a rough, strong voice, excellent guitar playing, wildly funny stories, songs about grief, lost lovers, the lonely muscle mass of the bodybuilder, through to wild Celtic folk tones. A affectionately mocking description of his get-up (worn-out tracksuit bottoms, scuffed patent shoes, a holey denim shirt, white ski socks). Thanks to the organisers, who bring Leven back “again and again”.

1998-10-24-nordlands-framtid-takk-for-si.kurz: Report on the Bodø concert of Thursday (22.10.1998) from the point of view of the Bodø fan Thor Arne Brekke (36), who was experiencing his third Leven concert.
inhalt: Report on the Bodø concert of Thursday (22.10.1998) from the point of view of the Bodø fan Thor Arne Brekke (36), who was experiencing his third Leven concert. He came to Leven through a free CD from the music magazine *Beat*. On the previous Bodø visit he paid the fan club subscription to Leven personally, but never received a CD or member newsletters; when he enquired, fan club head Mick Nolan replied that one must not give Leven money, as it disappears at once. Leven, forewarned by Nolan, reassured him when they met again that the CD was coming. The concert itself: Leven alone on a stool, strong melodies, humorous travel stories, around 90 attentive listeners.

1998-10-24-nordlandsposten-stakkars-jack.kurz: A scolding of the audience over the concert at Den Siste Glæde on Thursday (22.10.1998, approx. 60 visitors, admission 60 kroner): about ten bellowing young men reduced Leven to background music at his own concert; the critic would have understood if Leven had sent them to hell, as Ole Paus once did, and misses any intervention by the staff. Despite the noise, Leven put his songs across with force and nerve and did his work professionally.
inhalt: A scolding of the audience over the concert at Den Siste Glæde on Thursday (22.10.1998, approx. 60 visitors, admission 60 kroner): about ten bellowing young men reduced Leven to background music at his own concert; the critic would have understood if Leven had sent them to hell, as Ole Paus once did, and misses any intervention by the staff. Despite the noise, Leven put his songs across with force and nerve and did his work professionally.

1998-10-26-bergensavisen-spirituell-berg.kurz: Conversation after Leven's course on “guitar-based songwriting” for local musicians at Hagstrøm (Ole Blues with Norsk Musikkråd).
inhalt: Conversation after Leven's course on “guitar-based songwriting” for local musicians at Hagstrøm (Ole Blues with Norsk Musikkråd). Leven says he made his professional debut in Bergen in 1967, together with an American gospel singer, and fell in love with the city at once; its “spiritual aura” is like coming home and reminds him of a small town on the Scottish west coast where he lived for a long time. Tours are normally just work for him – except in Bergen, where he always takes a day off. On Friday he comes to Garage with the “virtuoso The Celtic Soulmen”, the only place where he wants to play in Bergen. The concert in Førde the day before was “a bit wild”, most of the guests drunk.

What became of the planned live album of the Doll by Doll concert at Garage in 1997, Leven does not know – he forgot about it, and it does not mean much to him, so many people record his concerts. He prefers to tour alone: in bands one person always gets depressed and infects the others until nobody is talking to anybody any more.

From the seminar: images are the most important thing, which is why he always carries a notebook; you should write with your heart and not analyse. He deliberately allows himself only one cliché per song, warns against “biblical” images such as deserts and suggests drastically more interesting alternatives; American country singers use so many clichés that it becomes surreal and therefore exciting (k. d. lang). Caption: Leven plays a 58-year-old guitar that once belonged to Doc Watson.

1998-10-30-bergensavisen-leven-om-inspir.titel: [Jackie Leven, in town for his concert, on his sources of inspiration]
1998-10-30-bergensavisen-leven-om-inspir.kurz: Short box on the day of the concert: Leven names Van Morrison, Lou Reed and Neil Young as important influences – “Madame George” has an incredibly vivid text, Morrison has become less interesting over the years, Reed's great period runs from *Transformer* to *Berlin*.
inhalt: Short box on the day of the concert: Leven names Van Morrison, Lou Reed and Neil Young as important influences – “Madame George” has an incredibly vivid text, Morrison has become less interesting over the years, Reed's great period runs from *Transformer* to *Berlin*. Surprisingly, Chet Baker is his favourite singer. He tends to like individual albums and songs rather than complete bodies of work: the last Grant Lee Buffalo record, Soweto samplers, even a few Ace of Base hits; his “label mate” Ani DiFranco wrote one of the best songs of the century with “Untitled Face”. He toured folk clubs with Elvis Costello before he “became Elvis”; *Imperial Bedroom* has much that is beautiful; Rocky Burnette is a personal favourite.

1998-11-soundi-night-lilies.kurz: Top rating (5 out of 5) in the Finnish music magazine, issue 11/1998, put online (the website's dates are contradictory: 28.07.2007 in the artist list, 17.10.2012 in the article).
inhalt: Top rating (5 out of 5) in the Finnish music magazine, issue 11/1998, put online (the website's dates are contradictory: 28.07.2007 in the artist list, 17.10.2012 in the article). Niemi knew Doll by Doll from the 70s and came late to Leven's solo work; *Night Lilies* combines Celtic roots with blues, rock, jazz and country, carried by tin whistle, fiddle and mandolin. Strongest are Leven's voice and the autobiographically tinged lyrics; a mature, timeless work with classic potential.

1998-12-22-lofotposten-ikke-helt-det-sam.kurz: The reviewer, who had experienced Leven live in Kabelvåg (cf. her review of 23.10.1998), finds the album decent, but not as compelling as the solo artist with a “tired acoustic guitar”: with several musicians, additional voices and a tidier concept the atmosphere is different – Scottish blue tradition, “pub pop” and solid quality, good for dark December evenings. She prefers Leven alone with stories, singing and guitar.
inhalt: The reviewer, who had experienced Leven live in Kabelvåg (cf. her review of 23.10.1998), finds the album decent, but not as compelling as the solo artist with a “tired acoustic guitar”: with several musicians, additional voices and a tidier concept the atmosphere is different – Scottish blue tradition, “pub pop” and solid quality, good for dark December evenings. She prefers Leven alone with stories, singing and guitar.

1998-cooking-vinyl-jackie-leven-intervie.kurz: Short label interview on *Night Lilies*: Leven explains the album title as a memory of a smell that takes him back to his 17th year, and the cover (Ferdinand Keller's homage to Böcklin's “Isle of the Dead”).
inhalt: Short label interview on *Night Lilies*: Leven explains the album title as a memory of a smell that takes him back to his 17th year, and the cover (Ferdinand Keller's homage to Böcklin's “Isle of the Dead”). He raves about the “Disastrodrome” festival at London's South Bank Centre under David Thomas and announces a duet EP with Thomas (“You've Lost That Lovin' Feeling”). He explains his success in Germany and Scandinavia by saying that music there is about “life, death and beauty”, in Britain about lifestyle. He pokes fun at major labels (the £200 lunch), plus joke answers (barman in Ireland; card game in a high-security prison with Rev Hammer and Martin Goldschmidt).

1998-muze-macmillan-larkin-encyclopedia-.titel: The Encyclopedia of Popular Music (entries “Doll By Doll” and “Leven, Jackie”)

1998-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.titel: [Collected finds from Nasjonalbiblioteket 1998: news items, announcements, lists]

1999-03-16-rockol-la-musica-in-televisio.kurz: The daily programme guide announces “Roxy Bar” on TMC2 at 8.30 pm with Jackie Leven, Puertorico, Carmen Consoli and Negrita.
inhalt: The daily programme guide announces “Roxy Bar” on TMC2 at 8.30 pm with Jackie Leven, Puertorico, Carmen Consoli and Negrita. This provides a contemporary programme record of an Italian television appearance on 16 March 1999.

1999-05-27-radio-bremen-konzert-club-mom.titel: [Radio Bremen: concert recording of Jackie Leven, Club Moments Bremen, 27.05.1999]
1999-05-27-radio-bremen-konzert-club-mom.kurz: Radio Bremen recorded Leven's solo performance at the Bremen music club “Moments” on 27 May 1999; MIG released it in 2024 as CD 1–2 of the box “Live Or Die – Live In Bremen 1999 & 2004” (“recorded by the broadcaster in the usual excellent sound quality”).
inhalt: Radio Bremen recorded Leven's solo performance at the Bremen music club “Moments” on 27 May 1999; MIG released it in 2024 as CD 1–2 of the box “Live Or Die – Live In Bremen 1999 & 2004” (“recorded by the broadcaster in the usual excellent sound quality”). Besides songs such as “Stranger on the Square”, “Call Mother a Lonely Field”, “Jim O'Windygates”, “Marble City Bar” and “Gylen-Gylen”, the recording contains several narrative passages (“Jackie Talking About Football”, “… Andy White”, “… His Son Simon”, “… St. Kitts & Nevis”). The pieces can be heard via the label and the YouTube Topic channel.

1999-3pbs-fm-brain-massage-jackie-leven.medium: 3PBS FM Melbourne, programme “Brain Massage” (recording on YouTube, channel Owlsley Burroughs)
1999-3pbs-fm-brain-massage-jackie-leven.kurz: A good 21 minutes of studio conversation with two live pieces, broadcast in Steve G. Mileham's programme “Brain Massage” on 3PBS FM Melbourne; the presenter uploaded the recording in 2022 under his stage name Owlsley Burroughs.
inhalt: A good 21 minutes of studio conversation with two live pieces, broadcast in Steve G. Mileham's programme “Brain Massage” on 3PBS FM Melbourne; the presenter uploaded the recording in 2022 under his stage name Owlsley Burroughs. Leven is on his second Australian trip, shortly after the first: by his own account he has come straight from a television programme with Bert Newton and goes back there afterwards, was at WOMADelaide and the Port Fairy Folk Festival, plays in Melbourne at the Continental and the Dan O'Connell, and travels on to WOMAD offshoots in Johannesburg and Auckland. He raves about Dan Penn and Spooner Oldham, says “Night Lilies” was made with “ruthless military precision”, explains the album title by the scent of night lilies on a Greek island that reminded him of a railway embankment in Scotland, and interprets the album as an arc spanning some 30 years of memory. He plays “Sick Harbour Lament” (the record company wanted to shorten the title) and, at the end, a second piece, tells the story of how “Elvis Green” came about (an American woman with a green vintage car, an interest in buying it on David Gilmour's part, her death the same night), describes the tension between dark lyrics and light music using Chet Baker as an example, and names John Cale/Terry Riley's “Church of Anthrax” as a model for “Carnival Dark”. Tone: relaxed promotional conversation rich in anecdotes; all stories are self-reports.

1999-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.titel: [Collected finds from Nasjonalbiblioteket 1999: news items, announcements, lists]

2000-01-26-bergensavisen-plate-jackie-le.kurz: Short, benevolent record review: a predominantly melancholy, resigned mood lies over the album.
inhalt: Short, benevolent record review: a predominantly melancholy, resigned mood lies over the album. The opening cover of “You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin'” sounds good but does not stand comparison with the Righteous Brothers; “Single Father”, by contrast, is probably the most beautiful song Leven has ever written (grey weather, fog, lost love, vanished industrial jobs), and “I Saw My Love Walk Into Clouds” is Scottish soul at its best. Notice of the concert on 1 March at the Bergen venue Den Stundesløse (“Stundik'en”).

2000-01-wandering-dog-defending-ancient-.titel: [Review of Defending Ancient Springs, start-of-year column]
2000-01-wandering-dog-defending-ancient-.medium: wandering.dog (private music site at Virgin Net)

2000-02-01-dagsavisen-liv-og-leven.kurz: Leven stays true to himself on the new album: emotionally charged songs about men, women and the great loneliness afterwards, opened by Phil Spector's “You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin'”.
inhalt: Leven stays true to himself on the new album: emotionally charged songs about men, women and the great loneliness afterwards, opened by Phil Spector's “You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin'”. Featured are David Thomas (Pere Ubu) on accordion and a band with former members of James, The Christians and Lighthouse Family. The strongest piece is perhaps the closing “Morbid Sky”, in fact a performance by David Thomas's Pale Orchestra with Leven in the line-up. Tone: very beautiful songs, but not different enough from the two “almost formidable” predecessors. Notice of the Oslo concert on 28 February and a subsequent Norwegian tour.

2000-02-03-the-daily-telegraph-the-lost-.kurz: Large portrait on the release of *Defending Ancient Springs*, Leven's sixth solo album for Cooking Vinyl, which McCormick considers perhaps his best.
inhalt: Large portrait on the release of *Defending Ancient Springs*, Leven's sixth solo album for Cooking Vinyl, which McCormick considers perhaps his best. Leitmotif: talent and fame have little to do with each other – Leven is the “great lost British rock star”. McCormick portrays Doll by Doll as the industry's hottest hope at one time, undone by a ruinous contract with Automatic; around 1982 Leven was solo and signed to Chrysalis. Leven tells of the attack in north London (choking, kicking, rescue by his producer in a Range Rover), the broken ribs, the injured larynx, almost 18 months without a voice, steroids with weight gain and the feeling of being “covered in electric fur”, then a year of heroin. Self-healing with acupuncture and “psychic healing” led in 1985 to the founding of the CORE Trust, whose centre Princess Diana opened. The girlfriend who had accompanied him through everything ran off with the Dalai Lama's bodyguard (Leven's punchline: she had met him as an acupuncturist). Leven reflects at length on the loss of his falsetto, which made him a terser, more considered writer, and on his position “more like a poet than a pop musician”, who has to make a brilliant record every 18 months. The connection to Robert Bly and the men's movement is mentioned. Tone: admiring, with blunt remarks about Leven's appearance (double chin, belly).
zitate_kontext: Leven on the consequences of the attack.

2000-02-07-wiseacre-defending-ancient-sp.kurz: Short review with a punchline: one should learn to skip track 1 by programming, because the opening version of “You've Lost That Loving Feeling” (with David Thomas) is bland.
inhalt: Short review with a punchline: one should learn to skip track 1 by programming, because the opening version of “You've Lost That Loving Feeling” (with David Thomas) is bland. The rest of the album shows Leven at his best, vocally and as a songwriter; “The Working Man's Love Song”, “Single Father” and “Your Winter Days” are singled out. Tone: positive with a clear reservation.

2000-02-08-nordlands-framtid-gode-sanger.kurz: Positive review from Bodø, where Leven is “topical” (concert announcement). Like Mike Scott and Van Morrison, Leven stands in the field of tension between American rock music and the folk music of the British Isles, without resembling either of the more famous ones.
inhalt: Positive review from Bodø, where Leven is “topical” (concert announcement). Like Mike Scott and Van Morrison, Leven stands in the field of tension between American rock music and the folk music of the British Isles, without resembling either of the more famous ones. Lyrics with an undertone of loneliness and longing, earthy, acoustically grounded arrangements; named are “Single Father”, “Paris Blues”, the harder “Morbid Sky” and the cover “You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin'” with guest David Thomas.

2000-02-09-hamar-dagblad-poetisk-musikk.kurz: Benevolent review: the little-known Scot presents his 18th album; the poetry lover writes darkly, simply and strikingly about love and misery, musically somewhere between folk, country and blues.
inhalt: Benevolent review: the little-known Scot presents his 18th album; the poetry lover writes darkly, simply and strikingly about love and misery, musically somewhere between folk, country and blues. Deliberate arrangements support text and melody; “a record that grows”. A box (“Nesten drept, fant kur”) summarises the familiar story: near-strangling in London in the early 80s, a year without a voice, heroin, a self-developed withdrawal cure (acupuncture, healing, reflexology), and from it The Core Trust; Princess Diana was among the supporters; Leven is active in the Men's Movement.

2000-02-18-glamdalen-en-fyr-uten-om-det-.kurz: Full-page portrait on the release of *Defending Ancient Springs*, according to a note at the end based on a text by Kjell Haglund in the magazine *Pop* (no. 24/1997).
inhalt: Full-page portrait on the release of *Defending Ancient Springs*, according to a note at the end based on a text by Kjell Haglund in the magazine *Pop* (no. 24/1997). The biography is told in Leven's version: born some 50 years ago among the dying coalfields of Fife, on the road at 18 as a hippie (Dorset, Madrid, Berlin, western Ireland), living for two months in an abandoned lighthouse on dog biscuits and water; in this period the “acid-soaked” album *Control* as John St. Field. Doll by Doll is compared with Television (long, complex songs, Verlaine-like poetry); after ever quieter records the band split up in 1983 out of exhaustion.

The attack is described like this: Leven was walking home at night with a freshly signed solo contract in his pocket when someone choked him from behind until he lay unconscious in the gutter; prescribed painkillers led to pill addiction, then heroin addiction. A withdrawal took him to little Argyll, where he recovered after a year of addiction and began writing again in 1985, while building up the CORE Trust. After a failed relationship he moved to London; meeting Robert Bly and his men's movement (*Iron John*, in Norwegian “Mannen”) shaped his career – five albums in four years – and spun on the Celtic thread of “Main Travelled Roads”. Musically he sounds like a sharpened Van Morrison at his best. Conclusion: Leven's life is the message that one can stumble and get up again.

2000-02-18-jaerbladet-jackie-leven-defen.titel: [Jackie Leven: Defending Ancient Springs – review with profile boxes]
2000-02-18-jaerbladet-jackie-leven-defen.kurz: Music page with a review and biographical boxes. The review is predominantly positive (folk music masterfully interwoven with poetic lyrics, calm sound), but criticises two pieces: “Keys to the Forest” is too heavy-hearted, the opening cover “You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin'” simply ugly.
inhalt: Music page with a review and biographical boxes. The review is predominantly positive (folk music masterfully interwoven with poetic lyrics, calm sound), but criticises two pieces: “Keys to the Forest” is too heavy-hearted, the opening cover “You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin'” simply ugly. Tips for a first listen: “Paris Blues”, “The Working Man's Lovesong”, “Defending Ancient Springs”. The boxes tell the biography (left Scotland at 18, *Control* as John St. Field, “only released in Spain?”, five records with Doll by Doll, “one never released”, attack, heroin, CORE Trust, friendship with Robert Bly, readings by Bly and Mike Scott on *The Mystery of Love*). Announcement: Sunday, 5 March, at Café Sting in Stavanger.

2000-02-28-gaesteliste-bodenstaendigkeit.kurz: First of five Gaesteliste interviews by Ullrich Maurer with Leven, on the release of “Defending Ancient Springs” (2000).
inhalt: First of five Gaesteliste interviews by Ullrich Maurer with Leven, on the release of “Defending Ancient Springs” (2000). Maurer introduces Leven as an “oddball” who found a home at Cooking Vinyl after Doll by Doll. Leven says he has rediscovered the magic of songwriting from his beginnings; as Doll by Doll's singer he was a boy, today he is a man. He explains the album title with the (pseudoscientific) idea that water has a memory: every person is born with a kind of inherited memory, which one defends in old age by reflecting on one's roots. He goes on to explain individual pieces: “Your Winter Days” is based on a folk song from Oban, “Hand Is Pale With Holy Kisses” on a poem by Marina Tsvetaeva, “You've Lost That Loving Feeling” is a dark, paranoid, underrated song; plus short poems from the Spanish. He relates that an American friend told him during his Berlin period that for the British it is never about travelling, but about homesickness and return. David Thomas (Pere Ubu), whom he got to know through “Mirror Man”, Maurer calls a kindred spirit; “Morbid Sky” from the project is on the album. “Paris Blues” goes back to a scene in a Paris café with Thomas (self-report). Tone: benevolent, slightly ironic towards Leven's philosophy.

2000-03-01-bergensavisen-berost-leven.kurz: Preview of the concert the same evening at Den Stundesløse (“Stundik'en”) with an interview. Leven (49) says he is lucky: nobody steers him, he is with a small company that lets him get on with it – quite unlike Van Morrison or Bob Dylan, who always have someone above them.
inhalt: Preview of the concert the same evening at Den Stundesløse (“Stundik'en”) with an interview. Leven (49) says he is lucky: nobody steers him, he is with a small company that lets him get on with it – quite unlike Van Morrison or Bob Dylan, who always have someone above them. The reviews of *Defending Ancient Springs* are overwhelming; Rolf Sejersted, who brought him back to Norway, sees him on the verge of the big breakthrough, and a big American label has offered him a contract – “then freedom is probably over”.

Asked whether “The Working Man's Lovesong” might be about the closure of the shipyard in Laksevåg, Leven answers that he believes everything goes in circles. His songs are more joy at having experienced something good than blues; he shares an African view of death as a reunion with the ancestors. Inspiration: poets, philosophers, Chet Baker, R. L. Burnside, Johnny Dowd and “David Munyan”, who inspired him to write “Single Father”. One should not analyse his music to death, but see the images. Turning 50 feels good, he never liked being young.

2000-03-02-nordlys-leven-med-leven.kurz: Telephone interview on the day of the concert in Tromsø (Blå Rock Café). Leven, with a cold, promises old songs (“easier to play”) alongside new ones.
inhalt: Telephone interview on the day of the concert in Tromsø (Blå Rock Café). Leven, with a cold, promises old songs (“easier to play”) alongside new ones. On the theme of *Defending Ancient Springs* he says that the “straight arrow of time” of the modern world troubles him; he likes the idea that time runs in a circle. The album is about the water you have in your body at birth and which is gradually replaced; all your life you long for it, and at death you should have the same water back. Where the idea came from he no longer remembers; he is interested in a holistic view of body and health.

On the tour: the Oslo concert went well, 260 spectators, he played “bloody well” but was nervous – it was his first concert since a gig in Pittsburgh in December; after a flu infection he even had to go to hospital. The day before had been the second tour concert, in Bergen. With its snow, Tromsø reminds him of the Scotland of his childhood, he would like to come in summer one day; he values Egon (Holstad) of the Blå Rock and the Grand Hotel, where he always stays, especially its bar.

2000-03-02-rogalands-avis-stilsikker-fra.kurz: Two texts by the same author on the same page. The review calls Leven a “crooked observer of life” with a rare talent; *Defending Ancient Springs* is rougher than usual, which is down to David Thomas (duet “You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin'”, “Morbid Sky” with David Thomas and the Pale Orchestra…
inhalt: Two texts by the same author on the same page. The review calls Leven a “crooked observer of life” with a rare talent; *Defending Ancient Springs* is rougher than usual, which is down to David Thomas (duet “You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin'”, “Morbid Sky” with David Thomas and the Pale Orchestra and Leven as singer); the title track and “Single Father” can stand many playthroughs. The preview “Jackie Leven til Stavanger igjen” announces the fourth Stavanger visit (Sunday, Sting Nere), describes the recording studio Bryn Derwen in Snowdonia (in the shadow of the world's largest slate quarry), quotes Brian Hinton (themes “love, violence, drinking and poverty”) and retells childhood in Fife, Doll by Doll, the attack, heroin and the CORE Trust.

2000-03-02-tromso-jackie-leven-vender-ti.kurz: Preview of Leven's fifth visit to Tromsø: he has, as probably the only international artist, mentioned Tromsø bars – first the Blå Rock Café, then the Grand bar – in acknowledgements on record sleeves.
inhalt: Preview of Leven's fifth visit to Tromsø: he has, as probably the only international artist, mentioned Tromsø bars – first the Blå Rock Café, then the Grand bar – in acknowledgements on record sleeves. Promoter Egon Holstad (Blå Rock Café, record shop Feedback) is pleased about the media attention: on Monday Leven was even on the NRK news *Dagsrevyen*; the critics are always enthusiastic, the record buyers have rather let him down. Short look back at Doll by Doll (four records 1979–82, declared geniuses by critics, overlooked by buyers).

2000-03-03-bergensavisen-gudbenadet-kar.kurz: Positive review of the solo concert at Den Stundesløse (01.03.2000): Leven had a stage authority that surpassed most singer-songwriters – with a “God-given” voice, acoustic guitar, a foot that kept time (microphone at foot level) and a loose tongue.
inhalt: Positive review of the solo concert at Den Stundesløse (01.03.2000): Leven had a stage authority that surpassed most singer-songwriters – with a “God-given” voice, acoustic guitar, a foot that kept time (microphone at foot level) and a loose tongue. The mostly autobiographical stories between the songs set him apart from others; humour always lay beneath the bittersweet episodes. A joke about Norwegians who always phone when you are sitting on the toilet – “that's surely Frank Nes (of Ole Blues)” – had the room laughing. A band was hardly missed.

2000-03-03-rolling-stone-de-defending-an.kurz: Feyer reviews the album as a meeting of two wilful characters (Leven and David Thomas, who met on the “Mirror Man” project at the Queen Elizabeth Hall).
inhalt: Feyer reviews the album as a meeting of two wilful characters (Leven and David Thomas, who met on the “Mirror Man” project at the Queen Elizabeth Hall). He praises the stripped-down version of “You've Lost That Loving Feeling”, which lays bare its paranoia, and the concentrated pieces (“Single Father”, “Working Man's Love Song”), less so the overloaded title song; “Hand Is Pale With Holy Kisses” sets Marina Tsvetaeva to music. Overall tone: appreciative with reservations.

2000-03-03-tonsbergs-blad-poeten-leven.kurz: Portrait distributed via the NTB Pluss agency at the start of the tour. The “friend of Norway” sees himself above all as a poet.
inhalt: Portrait distributed via the NTB Pluss agency at the start of the tour. The “friend of Norway” sees himself above all as a poet. It recounts the near-death after a mugging in the early 80s (almost strangled, without a voice for over a year), then heroin – and his girlfriend running off with the Dalai Lama's bodyguard. His 18th album has now been released; the European tour began “this week” at John Dee in Oslo and continues to Bergen, Tromsø, Trondheim and Stavanger.

Leven says he does not know exactly why he starts in Norway; he likes the country at this time of year, especially Tromsø; he has never played in Norway or Sweden in good weather. He likes the Norwegian audience, even if it is sometimes rather drunk, especially in Bodø and Kabelvåg. He takes it as a compliment that he is called the great lost British rock star: in every generation some get lost, he lost commercially, but he is more a poet than a rock star and only ever wanted to play in a rock band. His boyhood wish to travel the world with a guitar has come true; he got lost and was found. He lives in a happy relationship with a jazz singer; “Single Father” is about his adult son.

2000-03-04-nordlys-grisete-sentimental.kurz: Review of the concert at Blå Rock Café on 02.03.2000: Leven was by turns hilariously funny – a coarse hotel-room anecdote in place of a television appearance – and tearfully sentimental, in sharp contrast to the poetry of his songs.
inhalt: Review of the concert at Blå Rock Café on 02.03.2000: Leven was by turns hilariously funny – a coarse hotel-room anecdote in place of a television appearance – and tearfully sentimental, in sharp contrast to the poetry of his songs. He has been travelling alone for years with a rickety guitar that is more a body part than an instrument; open D tuning and virtuoso fingerpicking with echoes of Delta blues and the Highlands recalled an acoustic Rory Gallagher. The quiet audience and the cramped room were a perfect match; recommendation to buy *Defending Ancient Springs*.

2000-03-04-tromso-en-opplagt-jackie-leve.kurz: Positive review of the solo concert on 02.03.2000 at Blå Rock Café: a “radiantly good-humoured” Leven with heartfelt performances of old and new songs, linked by witty, sly stories; an intimate, quiet atmosphere, disturbed only by one drunk.
inhalt: Positive review of the solo concert on 02.03.2000 at Blå Rock Café: a “radiantly good-humoured” Leven with heartfelt performances of old and new songs, linked by witty, sly stories; an intimate, quiet atmosphere, disturbed only by one drunk. The reviewer has known the records since 1994 but was seeing Leven live for the first time: a folksy presence, Celtic melancholy without excess weight, a solid guitarist.

2000-03-16-haugesunds-avis-lavmaelt-og-m.kurz: Leven has by now become a “friend of Norway” with a fabulous voice and a love of storytelling, somewhere between Celtic music, rock and folk.
inhalt: Leven has by now become a “friend of Norway” with a fabulous voice and a love of storytelling, somewhere between Celtic music, rock and folk. The album offers quiet, melodic songs between American rock à la John Hiatt and Scottish heritage, garnished with sound backdrops from experimental music. The reviewer found the cover “You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin'” and the sentimental “Single Father” less successful; the gems were “Paris Blues”, “Keys to the Forest” and “Morbid Sky”.

2000-03-25-westfaelische-rundschau-die-g.kurz: Review of the concert at the “Zeche” in Bochum in March 2000 by Bernd Berke, then arts editor of the Westfälische Rundschau (Dortmund); the text is in the archive of his blog Revierpassagen (archive texts from 1974).
inhalt: Review of the concert at the “Zeche” in Bochum in March 2000 by Bernd Berke, then arts editor of the Westfälische Rundschau (Dortmund); the text is in the archive of his blog Revierpassagen (archive texts from 1974). Berke describes an audience of initiates calling out for “Single Father”, Leven's voice with a “Pavarotti range” and a guitar that “speaks all languages”; the songs come mainly from “Forbidden Songs” and “Defending Ancient Springs”. “Paris Blues” and “You've Lost That Loving Feeling” are singled out; Deborah Greenwood (vocals) and Michael Cosgrave (keyboards) also appear. Overall tone: enthusiastic, and he finds it incredible that such an artist should still count as an insider tip.

2000-04-05-bergensavisen-i-arkiv-forbidd.kurz: In the “I arkiv” column, Tore Bø recommends the 1995 album: *Defending Ancient Springs* is, for him, the best album of the year, and the recent Bergen concert was his first Leven concert – a “middle-aged heavyset man in Harry clothes” alone with a guitar, who hit him straight in the soul.
inhalt: In the “I arkiv” column, Tore Bø recommends the 1995 album: *Defending Ancient Springs* is, for him, the best album of the year, and the recent Bergen concert was his first Leven concert – a “middle-aged heavyset man in Harry clothes” alone with a guitar, who hit him straight in the soul. Now he is looking for forgotten gems: some consider *Forbidden Songs* his best album; Leven stands between Van Morrison and John Martyn. Singled out: “Young Male Suicide”, “Some Ancient Misty Morning”, “The Wanderer”; further recommendations are *The Mystery of Love* (1994) and *Night Lilies* (1998).

2000-08-05-sydney-morning-herald-celtic-.kurz: Australian review on the release there of *Defending Ancient Springs*: “Scottish new wave folk meets Cleveland post punk”.
inhalt: Australian review on the release there of *Defending Ancient Springs*: “Scottish new wave folk meets Cleveland post punk”. Elder describes Leven as a mature songwriter who has left punk excess behind and embraced folk, the men's movement and serious lyric poetry, and places him between Van Morrison, Mike Scott, Yeats and Heaney – a modern, unvarnished Celticism of pain, alcohol, poverty and industrial ruins. He praises the juxtaposition of sweetness and abrasiveness, the shared vocals with David Thomas (“Paris Blues”) and, in particular, the eccentric version of “You've Lost That Loving Feeling”. Overall tone: clearly positive, the best album since *Fairytales For Hardmen*.

2000-09-21-head-heritage-doll-by-doll-gy.kurz: Enthusiastic fan retrospective on the second Doll by Doll album (1979). Furgess recalls a strange Melody Maker interview from 1979 in which Leven admitted heavy LSD use in the band and claimed to hear voices and communicate with the dead – the reason he bought *Remember*.
inhalt: Enthusiastic fan retrospective on the second Doll by Doll album (1979). Furgess recalls a strange Melody Maker interview from 1979 in which Leven admitted heavy LSD use in the band and claimed to hear voices and communicate with the dead – the reason he bought *Remember*. *Gypsy Blood* is one of his favourite albums of all time; he compares it with Traffic, John Cale, Moby Grape, Family and Love, and Leven's voice with a cross between Scott Walker and Tim Buckley, goes through it track by track (“Highland Rain” as the high point) and ends by noting that Leven has recovered from his heroin addiction and is touring again.

2000-09-26-the-independent-jackie-leven-.kurz: Review of an evening of songs with Leven, Andy White and Michael Weston King at the Purcell Room. Martin pans King (“borderline pomposity”) and finds White harmless; Leven, by contrast, is a huge talent.
inhalt: Review of an evening of songs with Leven, Andy White and Michael Weston King at the Purcell Room. Martin pans King (“borderline pomposity”) and finds White harmless; Leven, by contrast, is a huge talent. He summarises the biography, praises *Defending Ancient Springs* as perhaps his best album and describes Leven on stage “like a fisherman at rest”: shorts, a cocktail of gin, vodka and ginger wine, coarse anecdotes about Patsy Kensit, Salman Rushdie and Will Oldham, plus “Chevin”, “Single Father” and, to finish, Van Morrison's “Madame George”. Conclusion: a cult artist who must be recognised as a “living treasure”.

2000-09-29-bergensavisen-kulttreff-pa-ga.kurz: Announcement of the duo UbuDoll (Leven and David Thomas) for 23 November at the Garage club in Bergen; the name refers to Pere Ubu and Doll by Doll.
inhalt: Announcement of the duo UbuDoll (Leven and David Thomas) for 23 November at the Garage club in Bergen; the name refers to Pere Ubu and Doll by Doll. A happening with vocals, guitars and accordion is promised. Quoted from the press release: both are loners, and it could remain a one-off. Thomas and Leven met four years ago in England, first worked together on Thomas's theatre project *Mirror Man* (premiere “last autumn” in London, with a record at the same time), then on *Defending Ancient Springs*.

2000-11-22-bergensavisen-leven-pa-garage.kurz: Preview of the UbuDoll concert on 23.11.2000 at Garage, according to the paper their third concert together.
inhalt: Preview of the UbuDoll concert on 23.11.2000 at Garage, according to the paper their third concert together. Leven promises to “break all the rules”. On David Thomas: one of the great American artists of the present, with a mysticism that many great musicians lack; both have a short fuse. He says he met him when he found out that Thomas lived on the English west coast – he phoned him because they were on the same label, they drank a lot of cognac and walked Thomas's dogs on the beach.

Leven says that on the night of the concert he should actually have been in Scotland at the “Spirit of Scotland” awards, where he is nominated as an ambassador of Scottish art; he doubts he will win and chooses Bergen – typical of him to be Scottish abroad and never popular at home. Scottish television made the documentary “East Coast Boy, West Coast Man” about him, filmed all over Scotland, plus a concert in Glasgow; since then he has no longer been “Jackie who?”. He recorded *Defending Ancient Springs* in Wales with an almost blind sound engineer with phenomenal hearing; the record sold well in Europe. Right after New Year he is going back into the studio with the same musicians and David Thomas. A second piece carries a short interview with Thomas (47), who thinks he remembers having been in Norway once before in the 80s.

2000-11-24-dagsavisen-kulthelt-for-sin-h.kurz: Preview of UbuDoll's Oslo appearance on 24.11.2000, at its core a conversation with David Thomas.
inhalt: Preview of UbuDoll's Oslo appearance on 24.11.2000, at its core a conversation with David Thomas. Both were cult bands on either side of the Atlantic 20 years ago; now there are two exclusive concerts in Norway. Thomas does not remember exactly how the collaboration began; he brought Leven in for *Mirror Man*, Leven brought him in for *Defending Ancient Springs*. Both come from dark, cold places – hence Norway. The concerts consist of each taking part in the other's songs; there are no new joint songs or pieces by the old bands, and a record is unlikely because so much of it is talking on stage.

2000-11-25-bergensavisen-trivelig-pa-gar.kurz: Review of the UbuDoll concert on Thursday, 23.11.2000, at Garage (half full): a quiet, bittersweet, comic “cuddle hour”.
inhalt: Review of the UbuDoll concert on Thursday, 23.11.2000, at Garage (half full): a quiet, bittersweet, comic “cuddle hour”. Thanks to an exemption from Bergen's licensing rules, the concert began at 21.30 in front of a rapt, adult audience. Leven with acoustic guitar, worn shirt and tracksuit bottoms tucked into his socks, Thomas in a butcher's apron with accordion, both on stools. It opened with “Morbid Sky”, played out at length like “Paris Blues”; in between came stories from Leven's life and Thomas's tragicomic poetry (comparisons with Tom Waits, Robbie Robertson). Encores without leaving the stage: “Call Mother a Lonely Field” and Van Morrison's “Cyprus Avenue”.

2000-11-28-puls-ubudoll-nerve-humor-og-e.kurz: Stener-Andersen describes an overwhelming, nearly two-hour performance by Leven and David Thomas as UbuDoll at John Dee in Oslo.
inhalt: Stener-Andersen describes an overwhelming, nearly two-hour performance by Leven and David Thomas as UbuDoll at John Dee in Oslo. He praises the audience listening with concentration, the simple instrumentation of guitar and accordion, and the alternation of poetry, melody and mutual banter.
